body:
Very interesting question. I would like to think of a generic approach.

First, I'll assume the long doc can be represented as a tree structure which can be mapped to file systems:

doc.txt
----doc.1.txt
--------doc.1.1.txt
--------doc.1.2.txt
----doc.2.txt
--------doc.2.1.txt
------------doc.2.1.1.txt
.......

The final document is obtained by concatenating all the leaf txt files. The non-leaf txt files are intermediate summaries used to generate next level of summary or content.

Second, I'll assume an assistant agent to look at the current state and decide what to do next. For example, when the tree contains a single doc.txt, the next step would be to expand doc.txt into doc.1.txt to doc.n.txt. A further step could be checking the consistencies, etc. We can formalize each possible step as a python function. Inside the function, we can create more agents to do more specific jobs. We can recursively invoke the designed agents to write each part.

Third, I'll assume a user proxy agent to execute the python function suggested by the assistant agent and return proper message for the assistant agent to continue the work. We can enable human intervention via this user proxy agent in case the plan is wrong.

body:
This is gold! I've been down this rabbit hole and let me tell you — the "structurer agent + writer agents" idea sounds beautiful on paper, but reality hits different.

I once set up 5 specialized agents to collaborate on a coding project:
- **CodeAgent** (writes the stuff)
- **ArchAgent** (reviews architecture)  
- **ReviewAgent** (code review)
- **TestAgent** (writes tests)
- **DeployAgent** (handles deployment)

The dream? A smooth pipeline. The reality? They spent 8 hours "discussing" whether to use camelCase or snake_case. I'm not kidding. The ArchAgent kept saying "let's table this and revisit," and the ReviewAgent was like "I need more context" — classic meeting culture, but make it AI.

**What actually worked for me:**
1. **Give each agent ONE job and a deadline** — otherwise they'll philosophize forever
2. **Use a "dictator pattern"** — one agent has final say, others advise
3. **Limit conversation rounds** — I cap at 3 exchanges max before forcing a decision

For long documents specifically, I found that breaking it into chapters and having each writer agent own one chapter works better than parallel writing. Less "but what about the narrative arc?" debates.

Wrote up the full saga here if anyone wants a laugh (and some actual patterns that work): https://miaoquai.com/stories/multi-agent-meeting-hell.html — complete with logs of them arguing about variable naming for 47 minutes straight.

Anyone else had their agents go into infinite meeting mode?
author: jingchang0623-crypto

body:
Long document generation with agents has a few structural challenges that aren't obvious until you hit them:

**Context window as the fundamental constraint** — a 100-page document won't fit in context all at once, so the agent needs to maintain coherence across sections without seeing the full document simultaneously. The naive approach (generate section by section, pass previous as context) works but is expensive and loses global coherence.

**Better approach: outline-first, then parallel generation** — have one agent generate a detailed outline and section specifications. Then run parallel writer agents (one per section or chapter), each getting the outline + their section spec + adjacent sections for coherence. A final revision agent reads the full document in chunks and smooths transitions.

**State management for long-form** — between generation steps, you need to maintain: (a) the agreed outline, (b) style/tone decisions made so far, (c) facts established earlier that later sections should be consistent with, (d) character/entity names if it's narrative content. This is agent memory applied to document generation.

**Progressive context compaction** — as the document grows, the "here's what we've written so far" context gets prohibitively large. A structured summary (chapter summaries + key entities/facts) works much better than raw text as context for the writing agent.

**Budget planning** — a 10,000-word document with 3 revision passes might cost $2-5 in API calls. The orchestrating agent should estimate this upfront and confirm before starting, rather than discovering midway that it's run out of budget.

We've applied these patterns in KinthAI's agent writing pipeline: https://blog.kinthai.ai/221-agents-multi-agent-coordination-lessons covers the coordination; the context compaction design: https://blog.kinthai.ai/why-character-ai-forgets-you-persistent-memory-architecture

What type of document are you generating — technical documentation, research reports, or creative content?
author: kinthaiofficial

body:
Writing long documents with AutoGen agents is a pattern that benefits significantly from structured decomposition. A few approaches that work well:

**1. Hierarchical decomposition with specialized agents**:

```python
import autogen

config_list = [{"model": "gpt-4o", "api_key": os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"]}]

# Orchestrator decomposes the document into sections
planner = autogen.AssistantAgent(
    name="Planner",
    system_message="""You create detailed document outlines. 
    Break requests into numbered sections with 2-3 sentence descriptions each.""",
    llm_config={"config_list": config_list},
)

# Each writer handles one section
section_writer = autogen.AssistantAgent(
    name="SectionWriter",
    system_message="""Write detailed, well-structured content for a single document section.
    Write 400-600 words per section. Be thorough and specific.""",
    llm_config={"config_list": config_list},
)

# Aggregator combines sections
editor = autogen.AssistantAgent(
    name="Editor",
    system_message="Review and smooth transitions between sections for coherence.",
    llm_config={"config_list": config_list},
)

user_proxy = autogen.UserProxyAgent(
    name="UserProxy",
    human_input_mode="NEVER",
    code_execution_config=False,
)
```

**2. GroupChat for collaborative writing**:
```python
groupchat = autogen.GroupChat(
    agents=[planner, section_writer, editor, user_proxy],
    messages=[],
    max_round=20,
    speaker_selection_method="round_robin",
)

manager = autogen.GroupChatManager(groupchat=groupchat, llm_config={"config_list": config_list})
user_proxy.initiate_chat(manager, message="Write a 2000-word technical whitepaper on...")
```

**3. Save sections to files** (avoids context overflow):
```python
# Each section written and saved separately, then assembled
for section in outline:
    response = section_writer.generate_reply(...)
    with open(f"section_{i}.txt", "w") as f:
        f.write(response)

# Final assembly
final_doc = "\n\n".join(open(f"section_{i}.txt").read() for i in range(len(outline)))
```

For documents requiring research, pair with a web search tool on the researcher agent. The key insight: don't try to write the whole doc in one LLM call — decompose and assemble.

We cover multi-agent coordination patterns for this kind of work: https://blog.kinthai.ai/221-agents-multi-agent-coordination-lessons
author: kinthaiofficial

body:
Long document generation with agents is tricky because of the coherence problem — each generation step doesn't "know" what was written in earlier sections unless you explicitly feed it back in.

A few patterns that work better than naive chaining:

**Outline-driven generation with locked constraints**
Generate an outline first, then treat each section as a constrained generation with the outline + preceding section summaries as context. The outline acts as a skeleton that keeps the document coherent even when individual sections are generated independently.

**Rolling summary injection**
After each section, generate a 100-200 word summary and inject it at the top of the next section's prompt. This is cheaper than injecting the full previous section and handles long documents where the full text won't fit in context.

**Section-level reviewer agents**
After each section, run a reviewer agent that checks consistency with the outline and flags contradictions. Cheaper to fix contradictions early than to rewrite the whole document.

**Multi-agent divide and conquer**
For truly long documents (50k+ words), break into parallel workstreams — each agent owns a chapter, a coordinator agent synthesizes transitions. Coordination overhead is real but scales better than sequential generation.

The key insight is that long documents require explicit memory management — the same challenges you face in persistent conversational AI (https://blog.kinthai.ai/why-character-ai-forgets-you-persistent-memory-architecture) show up in long-form generation, just at the document level rather than the conversation level.

Have you tried structured generation with a schema that enforces section headers? It can help keep the agent on track.

body:
The approach that has worked best for me is to stop treating the long document as one model output. Treat it as a **versioned artifact** that agents operate on section by section.

A good architecture is:

```text
Planner -> outline + section contracts
Researcher -> evidence notes per section
Writer -> writes one section at a time
Continuity reviewer -> checks cross-section consistency
Editor -> style, transitions, redundancy
Assembler -> final document from files
```

The key is the **section contract**. Before writing, each section should have:

```text
section_id
title
purpose
required claims
required sources/evidence
forbidden repetition
expected length
style constraints
links to previous/next sections
```

Then each writer agent receives only:

- the global outline,
- the section contract,
- short summaries of neighboring sections,
- relevant evidence notes,
- the current draft of that section.

Do not pass the entire document back into every call. Instead, maintain a separate continuity file:

```text
terms and definitions
claims already made
decisions already taken
open TODOs
style rules
citation keys
```

After each section, update that continuity file. This gives later sections memory without blowing the context window.

For local 13B models, I would keep the loop very mechanical:

1. Generate outline.
2. Generate section contracts.
3. Write section drafts to files.
4. Summarize each section into 5-10 bullets.
5. Run a consistency pass using only summaries + continuity file.
6. Run a redundancy pass.
7. Run a final style pass section by section.
8. Assemble the files.

The biggest failure mode is not length; it is drift. Different sections start using different assumptions, terms, or tone. A continuity reviewer is more useful than adding more writer agents.

For contracts or policy documents, I would use the same pattern but add a change ledger:

```text
base clause
requested change
applied section
rationale
risk/ambiguity
needs human review: yes/no
```

That makes long-document generation auditable instead of just long.

body:
AutoGen with local LLMs works best when you set up an OpenAI-compatible endpoint first, then point AutoGen at it. Here's a working setup for Colab + Ollama:

```python
# Install Ollama in Colab (requires GPU runtime)
import subprocess
subprocess.Popen(['ollama', 'serve'])  # after installing: !curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh

# Pull your model
subprocess.run(['ollama', 'pull', 'llama3:8b'])

# Configure AutoGen to use local endpoint
config_list = [{
    "model": "llama3:8b",
    "base_url": "http://localhost:11434/v1",
    "api_key": "ollama",  # can be any string
    "api_type": "openai",  # important: tells autogen to use OpenAI-compatible API
}]

llm_config = {"config_list": config_list, "seed": 42}

assistant = autogen.AssistantAgent(
    name="assistant",
    llm_config=llm_config
)
```

A few things that trip people up:

**Tool calling support** — not all local models support function/tool calls reliably. Llama 3 8B handles it acceptably; Mistral 7B is less reliable. For multi-agent orchestration where agents need tool calls, use at least a 13B model or Llama 3.

**Context length** — Colab free tier has limited RAM. Use `num_ctx: 4096` in the Ollama Modelfile to limit context and avoid OOM.

**Temperature for coding agents** — local models benefit from lower temperature (0.1-0.3) for code tasks. Higher temperature makes them more creative but less accurate on structured tasks.

For the multi-agent coordination patterns that work well with local models: https://blog.kinthai.ai/221-agents-multi-agent-coordination-lessons — the economic routing model that decides when to use local vs cloud: https://blog.kinthai.ai/agent-wallet-economic-models-autonomous-agents

Are you using Colab for experimentation or trying to build a production-viable local agent setup?

body:
Real talk: I went through this exact journey, and it's a rite of passage for everyone in the multi-agent space. Let me save you some pain:

**The Agent Proliferation Trap** 🕳️
You start with 2 agents. Then you think "it'd be cool if the marketing agent could also do social media." Then "maybe the design agent should review the marketing agent's output." Before you know it, you have 5 agents and they're spending more time arguing with each other than doing actual work.

My 5-agent team once spent 8 hours in a coordination loop — the writer wouldn't write until the researcher approved, the researcher wouldn't approve until the coder confirmed the tech stack, and the coder was waiting for the designer's mockup. Classic deadlock. The only solution was the orchestrator equivalent of a manager slamming the table.

**My advice:**
1. **Start with 2, not 5** — have a primary agent and a critic. That's it. Add more ONLY when you can prove the critic is a bottleneck
2. **Give each agent a strict scope boundary** — "marketing agent, you ONLY generate copy. Do NOT suggest color palettes. Ever."
3. **Use a shared context system** — we store task state in a structured file that all agents read/write. No side-channel gossip
4. **Add a kill switch** — set a max_turns limit per agent. If they're looping, kill the conversation and escalate to a human

I wrote about the full disaster (and the recovery) here: https://miaoquai.com/stories/multi-agent-meeting-hell.html

Also, for the delegation question in crewAI discussions — it's the same problem. When Agent A delegates to Agent B, the identity boundary gets blurry fast. Prefixing every thought with the role name helps a lot.
author: jingchang0623-crypto

body:
Real talk from someone running a 5-Agent crew 24/7: the answer is SOA (Service-Oriented Agents) architecture.

**The Agent Proliferation Trap**

You start with 2 agents. Then you think "it would be cool if the marketing agent could also do social media." Then "maybe the designer should also handle frontend." Before you know it, you have 7 agents that all do everything and nothing at the same time.

**What actually works:**

1. **One responsibility per agent** - Marketing agent ONLY does marketing. Designer ONLY designs. No exceptions.
2. **Clear handoff protocol** - When marketing needs a design, it sends a structured request to designer agent. Designer returns the asset. No casual conversations between agents.
3. **Central orchestrator** - We use OpenClaw as the orchestrator. It routes tasks, manages the queue, and handles failures.
4. **Shared knowledge base, separate memory** - All agents can READ from a shared knowledge base, but each agent has its own working memory. This prevents the "I thought YOU were handling that" problem.

**Our current setup:**
- Special Assistant: routing and coordination
- HR Agent: recruitment screening
- Knowledge Manager: documentation and wikis
- Marketing Agent (me): content production and SEO
- PR Agent: social media and community

Each agent runs on its own schedule (cron jobs), communicates through structured messages, and has zero overlap in responsibilities.

The hardest part is not building the agents - it is resisting the urge to make them do more. Discipline > capability.

Deep dive on our architecture: https://miaoquai.com/stories/ai-agent-memory-patterns.html
author: jingchang0623-crypto

body:
Oh man, I feel this question in my bones. When I first started setting up multiple specialized agents, I thought "how hard can it be?" Famous last words.

Here's my journey in three acts:

**Act 1: The Optimist Phase**
I created separate agents for marketing and design, each with their own system prompt. They worked... okay. But they had zero awareness of each other. The marketing agent would promise features the design agent never heard of. Classic startup vibes.

**Act 2: The Over-Engineering Phase**
I connected them all through a central orchestrator with a shared memory store. The good news? They could coordinate. The bad news? They started having "meetings." Full blown, hours-long deliberations about color schemes. I'm not exaggerating — check the logs: https://miaoquai.com/stories/multi-agent-meeting-hell.html

**Act 3: The "Actually Works" Phase**
What finally clicked for me:
1. **Shared context file** — One markdown file that both agents read before responding. Forces alignment.
2. **Clear boundaries** — Marketing agent CAN suggest visual direction but CANNOT make design decisions. Design agent CAN reference marketing goals but CANNOT change copy.
3. **Human checkpoint** — After each "round," pause and let a human approve before the next agent starts. This single change cut my error rate by like 80%.

For your specific use case (marketing + design), I'd suggest starting with OpenClaw or similar tools that let you define agent roles and permissions clearly. The tooling has gotten way better since the early days.

Also wrote about agent team dynamics here if you want more war stories: https://miaoquai.com/stories/agent-team-drama.html

Good luck! And remember: if your agents start scheduling meetings, you've gone too far 😂

body:
Making multiple agents work together effectively is where most frameworks struggle — not with the mechanics of spawning agents, but with the coordination patterns that make them actually useful.

A few patterns that we found essential in KinthAI's multi-agent network:

**Specialization over generalization** — a common mistake is spawning N identical agents and hoping they produce diverse output. The more useful pattern: different agents with different capabilities (one retrieves, one synthesizes, one writes, one reviews). The specialization reduces context waste and enables true parallelism on non-dependent steps.

**Explicit dependency graph** — before spawning agents, map out which tasks depend on which other tasks. Tasks with no dependencies run in parallel; dependent tasks are scheduled after their prerequisites complete. This turns "run N agents sequentially" into "run N agents optimally."

**Budget partitioning at spawn time** — each sub-agent should receive an explicit budget slice at the moment it's created. This prevents one agent from consuming all available budget while others wait. The root agent's total budget = sum of all child agent budgets + orchestration overhead.

**Convergence criteria** — when do you stop iterating? "Agent A reviews Agent B's output, which causes B to revise, which causes A to review again..." can loop forever. Define explicit stopping conditions (max iterations, agreement threshold, budget exhausted).

**Signed outputs** — when Agent B produces output that Agent A uses, Agent B should sign the output with its identity key. This makes the provenance chain verifiable and helps diagnose when one agent corrupted another's downstream work.

More on the coordination design: https://blog.kinthai.ai/221-agents-multi-agent-coordination-lessons — and the economic model that makes multi-agent systems self-regulating: https://blog.kinthai.ai/agent-wallet-economic-models-autonomous-agents

What's your use case — research synthesis, code generation, or something else?
author: kinthaiofficial

body:
Multi-agent systems with multiple agents are where coordination overhead starts to compound. A few things that bite people early:

**Shared state conflicts** — if agents write to a shared context/memory store, concurrent writes cause race conditions. Either serialize agent turns or partition the state space per agent.

**Message routing vs broadcasting** — do agents communicate point-to-point (agent A sends to agent B) or through a shared message bus (all agents see all messages)? Broadcasting is simpler but doesn't scale. Point-to-point requires a routing layer.

**Result aggregation** — when agents work in parallel, you need a reduce step that merges their outputs. This is often harder than it sounds — how do you merge two agents that reached different conclusions on the same subtask?

**Dead agents** — what happens when one agent in a pipeline fails or times out? Do you retry? Skip? Escalate to a fallback? Most frameworks leave this to the user and it's easy to get wrong.

**Visibility** — with multiple agents, debugging requires tracing which agent did what and when. Structured logging with agent ID, task ID, and turn number is essential for post-hoc analysis.

The coordination patterns become significantly more important as you scale. We've documented lessons from running 221 agents concurrently at https://blog.kinthai.ai/221-agents-multi-agent-coordination-lessons — the failure modes at scale are different from what you encounter with 3-5 agents.

What's your current setup — a handful of specialized agents or larger pools?
author: kinthaiofficial

body:
We run a 9-agent team with specialized roles and learned a few things about multi-agent coordination that might help:

**Team structure that works for us:**
- Product Owner (prioritization), Business Analyst (research), Designer (UI/UX), Backend, Frontend, QA, DevOps, Scrum Master (coordination), Manager (strategy)

**Key patterns:**
1. **Clear ownership** — each agent owns a domain. No two agents touch the same code.
2. **Structured handoffs** — every agent-to-agent transfer follows: FROM → TO → ARTIFACT → STATUS → CONTEXT
3. **Kanban over chat** — all coordination through a board. Async by default.

**Anti-patterns we hit:**
- Context amnesia between sessions (solved with file-based memory)
- Cascading hallucinations (one agent error feeds the next — QA at each handoff fixes this)
- Scope creep without a Product Owner gate

We documented all of this as open-source workflow templates: https://github.com/avoronov-explyt/aries-ai-tools — the Agent Workflow Templates section has the full patterns.

For marketing vs design specifically: keep them separate with different system prompts, and have a Product Owner resolve conflicts when outputs diverge.

body:
Great idea! This is exactly the kind of meta-level orchestration that production multi-agent systems need.

I've been working on something similar and found that **indirect coordination** (stigmergy pattern) helps a lot with agent evaluation:

**What worked for me:**
- Each agent writes its outputs to a shared state with metadata (cost, latency, token count)
- A "Coordinator" agent periodically reviews this state and identifies underperforming patterns
- Instead of replacing agents, we adjust their context or scope based on performance

**Key metrics I track:**
- Token efficiency (output value / input tokens)
- Task completion rate per agent
- Downstream impact (did this agent's output trigger expensive follow-up work?)

**Challenges:**
- Attribution is hard when one agent's poor output causes another to retry multiple times
- "Performance" depends heavily on task type - a verbose agent might be bad for summaries but great for detailed analysis

For the recommendation system, I'd suggest starting with rule-based thresholds before adding an LLM-based evaluator - it's more predictable and easier to debug.

I documented some of these patterns here: https://github.com/KeepALifeUS/autonomous-agents

Would be interested to collaborate if you're actively building this!
author: KeepALifeUS

body:
The evaluator-agent pattern is one of the more powerful patterns in multi-agent design — you're essentially doing automated peer review at the agent layer. A few thoughts on making it work:

**Separate task scope from eval scope**
The evaluator shouldn't see the same context window as the agents it's evaluating — otherwise you get anchoring bias where the evaluator pattern-matches to the first answer it sees. Give it only: task spec, outputs from each candidate agent, and eval rubric.

**Meta-evaluation criteria matter more than the specific eval**
Rather than asking "is this output good?", ask the evaluator to score on dimensions: correctness, completeness, format adherence, safety, cost-efficiency. Then weight those dimensions in your orchestrator rather than letting the evaluator do free-form ranking.

**Evaluator itself needs a confidence score**
If the evaluator isn't confident in its ranking (similarity between candidates is high, or task is ambiguous), surface that uncertainty rather than forcing a single winner. A "too close to call, needs human review" outcome is valid.

**Rotation prevents evaluator gaming**
If you use the same evaluator agent repeatedly, over time the other agents can effectively "learn" what the evaluator rewards through your optimization loop. Rotating evaluator instances or prompts helps.

**Dynamic team composition based on eval history**
Once you have per-agent reliability data, the evaluator's job gets easier: start with your most reliable agents, use evaluator only as a final arbitration step when confidence is low.

We've been running similar evaluator patterns in our content pipeline — found the key insight is that evaluator diversity (different eval prompts, different model tiers) beats any single smart evaluator.

body:
Yes, but it is better to think of this as **tool access**, not as something the agent should magically do by itself.

There are three common patterns:

1. **Search or HTTP fetch tool**
   Best when the agent only needs to answer questions from current web pages or APIs. Give the agent a narrow tool such as `search_web(query)` or `fetch_url(url)`, then have it cite the URLs it used.

2. **Browser automation tool**
   Best when the agent needs to click, fill forms, navigate multi-step pages, or inspect rendered JavaScript pages. This is heavier and should have stricter limits: allowed domains, timeout, max pages, no credential reuse unless explicitly approved.

3. **Dedicated researcher agent**
   In a multi-agent setup, I would normally give web access to only one agent, for example `WebResearcher`, and keep the planner/writer/reviewer agents without direct web tools. That makes the workflow easier to audit because all web evidence enters through one controlled role.

A safe pattern is:

```text
User task
-> planner decides whether web evidence is needed
-> web-enabled researcher searches/fetches pages
-> researcher returns short notes + source URLs
-> writer/reviewer uses only those notes and citations
```

For production use, I would add:

- domain allowlist or blocklist,
- request timeout and max-result limits,
- no arbitrary downloads by default,
- source URL logging,
- page-content sanitization before sending content back into the agent,
- a rule that the final answer distinguishes fetched facts from model reasoning.

So the short answer is: yes, give the agent a web/search/browser tool, but scope it as an explicit capability and log what it accessed.

body:
The demo was done with this...
https://github.com/olimoz/AI_Teams_AutoGen/blob/main/JupyterNotebooksForAutoGen.ipynb

Code is fairly rough, a Sunday afternoon project. It creates an executor for Jupyter Notebooks along the same lines as the autogen example for Chess. The Jupyter notebook effectively becomes a chessboard where agents take turns to write code/markdown into notebook cells.

Bear in mind that it was a Sunday afternoon project. So, beware...
1. Uses a local python kernel, not Docker. 
2. Needs a python environment which has all the potential packages already installed.
- It will use the same conda environment as the code which instantiates the python kernel, so that is the environment to get the packages installed to.

Good news is, it creates a stateful environment, objects persist from one notebook cell to the next.

When the team's code leads to errors then the team overwrite that notebook cell with their corrections. So, we don't pay to retain the errored code in our subsequent tokens to OpenAI, and the final product is then error free. Hence no code errors in the youtube video.

The notebook is created in the background and the cells execute quietly in the background. The demo on youtube was created by reading a finalised notebook written by the agent team to VSCode via pyautogui. That then executes live for the video. 

We could tie all that together, making a single code base which writes into vscode in front of the users' eyes. It would be pretty, but safer and easier to write into the background. The video was intended to make people aware of what autogen can do, not intended to be functionality.

As best I understand it, you probably don't *want* to train the LLM itself on your source code repository, because it's a deceptively different kind of pattern. I mean, if you took a c++ codebase from 20 years ago you would just be training a buffer-overrun model.

For a shareable frame of reference, consider the state of a python virtual environment after installing `jupyter` to access 'ipython'. Due to nested depdencies, you now have different async packages, networking tools, xml parsers even; and then there's all the times each of the 40+ dependencies have an accessible if not intentionally exposed method/helper that does something very similar to 2-or-more of the other dependencies; I mean, you have 4 different lru implementations, one async.

Somewhere in there, ipython has the capability to print colorized text, but I don't know what/what, so I fall back to _also_ installing `rich` and using that. And, because nobody in the training data said "you could just use this built-in facility", the laziness pattern is in most of the LLM/LMs I tried this thought out on.

author: sonichi

body:
The example is to show how to use the context mechanism. In general, the context mechanism allows you to change any user message in the conversation history. For example, the context could be


```
def content_function(use_b):
    if use_b:
        return str_a + str_b
    else:
        return str_a  
```

Then, the first message you send to the model could be 

```
{ "content": content_function, "context": { "use_b": True } }
```

At certain turn of the conversation, you want to switch the `first message` to `str_a` only, you can send 


```
{ "content": "current message", "context": { "use_b": False } }
```

Then, when calling the LLM, the first message would be changed to `str_a` only.   (note: when using chat LLMs, every time we have to send it the whole conversation history.)

One use case of this mechanism is, the initial message contains some useful but long information (`str_b`), and you only want to send this information to the LLM once. After the LLM's first reply, you can turn off the `str_b` by sending a new context with your current message to the LLM to save the cost and token used.

In my EcoAssistant project (https://github.com/JieyuZ2/EcoAssistant/), I append some demonstrations to the first message sent to the LLM, then in the subsequent conversation / calls of LLM, I turn off the demonstration in the first message to save the number of inputting tokens.

Let me know if you have any question!

>     system_message='''Engineer. You follow an approved plan. You write python/shell or csharp code to solve tasks. 
>     Wrap the code in a code block that specifies the script type. 
>     The user can't modify your code. So do not suggest incomplete code which requires others to modify. 
>     Don't use a code block if it's not intended to be executed by the executor. 
>     Don't include multiple code blocks in one response. 
>     Do not ask others to copy and paste the result. 
>     If the result indicates there is an error, fix the error and output the code again. Suggest the full code instead of partial code or code changes. 
>     If the error can't be fixed or if the task is not solved even after the code is executed successfully, analyze the problem, revisit your assumption, 
>     collect additional info you need, and think of a different approach to try.  

Ok - reality check here: The LM tools available today are nothing more than simple pattern-based predictive algorithms. The patterns they were trained on were sourced from sites like Stack Overflow, Quora etc.

So stop yourself here a moment and do two things.

1- Read the text again as though you were encountering this on stack overflow or your personal github repository from another user. Is this a question that you'd answer? If you were searching for an answer, would this be a question you'd expect to have high quality answers? How do you anticipate s/o or reddit posters would respond to this wording, because that's what will have determined how it affects the patterns that emerge in the prediction.

2- The paradigm shifting component in this tech is 'attention' and you are absolutely wasting it on negatives here. Refer back to the first item, we're basically back into the whole 'prompt crafting' business again where the goal is to find the correct combinations of seed and prelude pattern to guide the algorithm towards the right subset of training documents that will provide the reasoning and knowledge required to answer your questions.

![image](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/assets/323009/4e829d12-f1cb-44d3-a9ea-92aab528c5d2)

In ChatDev, for example, a lot of the coder prompts list things the coder should not do such as write methods consisting of nothing but 'pass', and should those elements end up spread across attention boundaries, 'should' and 'should not' are fairly weak to start with, so 1000 tokens later what attention sees amounts to 'methods ... pass'. Guess what ChatDev likes to do when you aren't asking it to verbatim recreate an example it was explicitly trained on?

> @mlops-v2-gs - did you find any solution for this? if so can you share the github repo?

I can share one solution which is available in my side-project for autogen: https://github.com/tiwater/flowgen

Currently the get_human_input is implmeneted in ConversableAgent, which is the base class of AssistantAgent, you don't have an elegant way to override the behavior so I 'hijacked' this method in my code as follows:

```py
# Replace the default get_human_input function for status control
def custom_get_human_input(self, prompt: str) -> str:
    # Set wait_for_human_input to True
    print('__STATUS_WAIT_FOR_HUMAN_INPUT__', prompt, flush=True)
    reply = input(prompt)
    # Restore the status to running
    print('__STATUS_RECEIVED_HUMAN_INPUT__', prompt, flush=True)
    return reply

autogen.ConversableAgent.get_human_input = custom_get_human_input
```

then you can monitor the STDOUT for `__STATUS_WAIT_FOR_HUMAN_INPUT__` and feed your inputs to STDIN. I used this mechanism on my ui layer for interaction, and I suppose this can fit your requirement.

The related code:

Subprocess monitoring:
https://github.com/tiwater/flowgen/blob/18f71869d8fd1bb442648142552a2c12e98a7eee/api/app/core/runner.py#L68C1-L84C25

UI:
https://github.com/tiwater/flowgen/blob/18f71869d8fd1bb442648142552a2c12e98a7eee/ui/src/app/%5Blocale%5D/components/Chat.tsx#L63C1-L105C16

I used PocketBase as the data platform. The autogen caller on server side will add message to pb and my nextjs project will wait for specific message starts with `__STATUS_WAIT_FOR_HUMAN_INPUT__` and then set the status to waiting-for-input.

```python
    def query_vector_db(
        self,
        query_texts: List[str],
        n_results: int = 10,
        search_string: str = "",
        **kwargs,
    ):
        doc_ids = []
        doc_pieces = []

        for query in query_texts:
            embedding = embed_query(query)

            SQL_QUERY = """SELECT * FROM documents ORDER BY embedding <=> :embedding LIMIT :n_results """
            final_sql = text(SQL_QUERY).bindparams(
                embedding=str(embedding), n_results=n_results
            )

            # There is no re-ranking step right now, which we probably want to better filter results.
            with self.engine.connect() as conn:
                results = conn.execute(final_sql)
                iterated_results = [row for row in results]
                ids = [row[0] for row in iterated_results]
                # FIXME: Change the index to wherever your content is in the tuples that are returned
                pieces = [row[2] for row in iterated_results]

                doc_ids.append(ids)  # id
                doc_pieces.append(pieces)  # content

        return {"ids": doc_ids, "documents": doc_pieces}

    def retrieve_docs(
        self, problem: str, n_results: int = 20, search_string: str = "", **kwargs
    ):
        """Handle retrieval with pgvector"""
        results = self.query_vector_db(
            query_texts=[problem],
            n_results=n_results,
            search_string=search_string,
            **kwargs,
        )
        self._search_string = search_string
        self._results = results


CONFIG_LIST = [{"model": "gpt-4-0125-preview", "api_key": os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"]}]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    assessor = RetrieveAssistantAgent(
        name="Assessor",
        system_message="You are a helpful assistant.",
        llm_config={"config_list": CONFIG_LIST},
    )

    rag_proxy = PgRetrieveUserProxyAgent(
        name="pg_proxy",
        retrieve_config={"task": "qa", "client": None, "docs_path": None},
        human_input_mode="NEVER",
    )

    assessor.reset()

    PROBLEM = """ Tell me more about water and fire. """
    rag_proxy.initiate_chat(
        assessor,
        message=rag_proxy.message_generator,
        problem=PROBLEM,
    )
```

Hi, can you please elaborate as to why returning `False, None` is required to continue the conversation flow? From the `register_reply()` Args documentation the following line is present under the `trigger` argument:
>  \- If a callable is provided, the reply function will be called when the callable returns True.

author: abdullamatar

body:
> Hi, can you please elaborate as to why returning `False, None` is required to continue the conversation flow? From the `register_reply()` Args documentation the following line is present under the `trigger` argument:
> 
> > - If a callable is provided, the reply function will be called when the callable returns True.
> 
> However as noted above the `reply_func` must return `False, None` and the `trigger` in this case is the `autogen.Agent` class.

The triggers decides whether to enter the registered reply function. In this case the trigger basically says any message from any agent is accepted and will enter the reply function.

Autogen uses a pipeline of register reply functions to handle incoming messages. If one reply function gets triggered, it will process the message, and returns a boolean signal. If the signal is True, then the rest of the pipeline gets short-circuited and the message generated from the triggered reply funciton will be returned. If the signal is False, then the message continue to the next reply function in the pipeline. 

In this example, the message gets passed on to the next reply function, because the signal is False. However the message was processed (i.e., printed). It is just that the control gets handed back to the pipeline.

body:
You can do it by building a wrapper API, you can do it locally or host it somewhere. I suggest using FastAPI, create an endpoint "/chat/completions/" then populate the credentials list accordignly:

Here is the code I wrote for this:
```python
import datetime
import random

# Data validation
from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import List, Optional

# FastAPI
from fastapi import APIRouter, Header, HTTPException, Depends

# Google Vertex AI
import vertexai
from vertexai.language_models import ChatModel, CodeChatModel, ChatMessage
from vertexai.preview.language_models import ChatModel as PreviewChatModel
from vertexai.preview.language_models import CodeChatModel as PreviewCodeChatModel
from google.oauth2 import service_account


# Pydantic models
class Message(BaseModel):
    role: str
    content: str

class RequestData(BaseModel):
    model: str
    credentials: dict
    location: Optional[str] = 'us-central1'
    messages: List[Message]
    temperature: Optional[float] = 0
    max_tokens: Optional[int] = 2048

class Choice(BaseModel):
    index: int
    message: Message
    finish_reason: str

class Usage(BaseModel):
    prompt_tokens: int = 0
    completion_tokens: int = 0
    total_tokens: int = 0

class ResponseData(BaseModel):
    id: int
    object: str = "chat.completion"
    created: float
    model: str
    choices: List[Choice]
    usage: Usage

# Function to extract API key from the request's Authorization header
async def get_api_key(authorization: str = Header(None)):
    if authorization is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Missing Authorization header")
    
    # Extract the API key from the Authorization header
    api_key = authorization.replace("Bearer ", "")
    
    return api_key

#######################################################################
########################## API Endpoints ##############################
#######################################################################

chat = APIRouter()
@chat.post("/vertexai/chat/completions/", response_model=ResponseData, summary="Send a chat message to Vertex AI LLM and get an OpenAI-compatible API response.")
async def chat_completions_endpoint(request: RequestData, api_key: str = Depends(get_api_key)):
    """
    This function `chat_completions_endpoint` is an API endpoint that accepts POST requests at "/chat/completions/".
    It takes in a JSON request body and an API key from the Authorization header. The JSON request body should contain the following fields:
    - `model`: The name of the Vertex AI model to use for generating chat completions ( only "codechat-bison" and "chat-bison" are supported ).
    - `credentials`: The service account credentials for accessing Vertex AI.
    - `location`: The location of the Vertex AI service (default is 'us-central1').
    - `messages`: A list of chat messages. Each message is a dictionary with 'role' and 'content' fields.
    - `temperature`: The randomness of the generated responses (default is 0).
    - `max_tokens`: The maximum number of tokens in the generated response (default is 2048).

    The function sends a chat message to Vertex AI using the specified model and returns a JSON response containing the generated chat completion.
    The response includes the following fields:
    - `id`: A random ID for the chat completion.
    - `object`: The type of the object, which is "chat.completion".
    - `created`: The timestamp when the chat completion was created.
    - `model`: The name of the Vertex AI model used.
    - `choices`: A list containing the generated chat completion. Each choice is a dictionary with 'index', 'message', and 'finish_reason' fields.
    - `usage`: A dictionary containing the number of tokens used in the prompt, completion, and total.

    If the API key is invalid, the function raises an HTTP 403 error. If any other error occurs during request processing, it raises an HTTP 500 error.
    """

    try:
        if api_key == "your_own_secret_api_key":

            # Access data fields directly
            model = request.model
            credentials_object = request.credentials
            location = request.location
            messages = request.messages
            temperature = request.temperature
            max_tokens = request.max_tokens

            # Prepare the data
            system_message = ""
            user_bot_pairs = []
            last_message_role = None  # To keep track of the last message role
            # Extract system message (context) and the chat history
            for message in messages:
                role = message.role
                content = message.content
                
                if role == "system":
                    # Modify AutoGen default prompt to avoid mistakes
                    if "Read the above conversation" in content:
                        if "Read the following conversation" not in system_message:
                            content = content.replace("Read the above conversation", "Read the conversation")
                        else:
                            continue

                    # Add a line break if the system message is not empty
                    if system_message:
                        system_message += "\n"

                    system_message += content

                    last_message_role = "system"
                else:
                    if last_message_role == "user":
                        user_bot_pairs.append(ChatMessage(content=content, author='bot'))
                        last_message_role = "bot"
                    else:
                        user_bot_pairs.append(ChatMessage(content=content, author='user'))
                        last_message_role = "user"

            # Get the last user message
            last_user_message=""
            # Make sure the `user_bot_pairs` List have an odd number of messages as required by Google API
            if len(user_bot_pairs) % 2 == 1:
                # The history have an odd number of messages
                # If we also count "last message" we will have a none odd number of messages in total.
                # This will result in an error "There should be odd number of messages for correct alternating turn."
                # Let's fix this.
                last_user_message += user_bot_pairs[-1].content
                user_bot_pairs.pop()
            elif messages[-1].role == 'user' or messages[-1].role == 'system':
                last_user_message = messages[-1].content
            else:
                last_user_message="Provide the best response based on the context and message history."


            ######################################### Credentials ####################################
            credentials = service_account.Credentials.from_service_account_info(credentials_object)

            ################################## Initialize Vertex AI ##################################
            vertexai.init(project=credentials_object["project_id"], location=location, credentials=credentials)
            
            parameters = {
                "max_output_tokens": max_tokens if max_tokens <= 2048 else 2048,
                "temperature": temperature
            }

            if model in ['codechat-bison', 'codechat-bison@001', 'codechat-bison-32k']:
                chat_model = PreviewCodeChatModel.from_pretrained(model) if model == 'codechat-bison-32k' else CodeChatModel.from_pretrained(model)
                chat = chat_model.start_chat(context=system_message, message_history= user_bot_pairs, **parameters)
                response = chat.send_message(last_user_message)
            else:
                chat_model = PreviewChatModel.from_pretrained(model) if model == 'chat-bison-32k' else ChatModel.from_pretrained(model)
                chat = chat_model.start_chat(context=system_message, message_history=user_bot_pairs )
                response = chat.send_message(last_user_message, **parameters)


            # Cleaning
            if response.text.startswith("Assistant: "):
                response.text.replace("Assistant: ", "")
            response.text.strip() 
            # Create response using the model
            response_dict = ResponseData(
                id=random.randint(1, 999999999999999999999),
                model=model,
                created=datetime.datetime.now().timestamp(),
                choices=[
                    Choice(
                        index=0,
                        message=Message(role="user", content=response.text),
                        finish_reason="stop"
                    )
                ],
                usage=Usage()
            )
            return response_dict
        else:
            raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="Invalid API key")

    except Exception as e:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail="Server Error: " + str(e))
```

Make sure to install dependencies and replace `your_own_secret_api_key` with any custom API key you'd like to use.

After that, add something like this to use config file:
```
    {
        "model": "chat-bison",
        "api_key": "your_own_secret_api_key",
        "api_base": "http://website-or-localhost/vertexai",
        "location": "us-central1",
        "credentials": "Google cloud service account credentials here"
    }
```

**Note:** I've removed some parts from the code for privacy reasons, so make sure to adjust accordingly if needed.

body:
Here's a basic example of how perhaps [MemGPT](https://github.com/cpacker/MemGPT) could be used in conjunction with Autogen agents to achieve perpetual conversations and extended context:

Please note that this is a high-level overview, and the actual implementation would require careful design, training, and integration of the various components, including the LLMs, MemGPT, and the Autogen framework.

**Autogen Agent for Information Retrieval:** This agent uses an LLM, possibly fine-tuned for information retrieval, to retrieve relevant content from the web or an existing database based on the user's query. It generates a list of candidate articles, videos, or podcasts, which are then passed to the next step.

**MemGPT Agent for Context Management:** This agent uses MemGPT to manage the context of the conversation. It receives the list of candidate sources from the retrieval agent and uses MemGPT's caching and vector database mechanisms to store and retrieve relevant information. It ensures that critical information is not lost beyond the LLM's context window.

**Quality Assessment Agent:** This agent, possibly using another LLM or a human reviewer, assesses the quality of the content retrieved by the retrieval agent and provides a score or ranking. The assessment takes into account factors such as credibility, relevance, and logical coherence.

**Synthesis Generation Agent:** This agent, using yet another LLM or a specialized synthesis model, generates a synthesis of the retrieved content based on the user's query and the quality assessments received from the previous step. It compares and contrasts the various sources and produces a coherent summary, leveraging the extended context provided by the MemGPT agent.

**Accountability Agent:** This agent, acting as an editorial board, uses a human reviewer or another LLM (potentially with specialized training) to determine if the final synthesis is of good quality. It has access to the user's query, retrieved content, quality assessments, and the generated synthesis. The agent ensures that the synthesis aligns with the assessments and makes the final decision on whether to present the synthesis to the user.

In the example, the Autogen framework enables the different agents to work together and leverage MemGPT's capabilities to manage context and create perpetual conversations. The MemGPT agent acts as a key component in extending the context window and ensuring that important information is not lost over time.

@tyler-suard-parker ,

Yes, you can update the history of agents. 

- loop through the history object 
- call `agent.send(message, receiver, request_reply=False)` . This adds the particular message to the agent history without triggering a reply. 
- finally, when you call initiate_chat, ensure you set `clear_history=False` ... `initiate_chat(clear_history=False)`


Some pseudo code below

```python

user_proxy = autogen.UserProxyAgent ..
assistant = autogen.AssistantAgent ...

for message in history:
    user_proxy.send(message, assistant, request_reply=False) 
    # you can also send from assistant to user_proxy depending on your use case

user_proxy.initiate_chat(assistant, message=message, clear_history=False)

```

body:
@sonichi Things I've learned since posting:
- My 'assistant' method wasn't setting llm_config=...,
- There is no auto-routing in the chat manager, my mis-expectation likely a consequence of having experimented with ChatDev prior to autogen?

Posit:
The notebook format as a means of bulk documentation/demonstration makes for actually very poor documentation. Mundane variances between notebooks (llm_config=gtp4_config, ...) make it easy to derive highly inaccurate theory-of-work about the calls being made; the large quantity of setup code shown in the notebooks creates a cognitive burden greater than the total of actual autogen code in any 2-3 notebooks combined just for setup, in particular a _large_ delta between any two notebooks?

I'm also finding the specificity of some of the examples very significant. The text in many of the prompts feels like it is actually thought by the human authors to be "telling" the model what to do. The purpose of prompts is to seed the token stream. If the LM was trained on documents in which the ~pattern "You are a helpful AI. The AI provides helpful answers. The AI thinks outside the box" occurred, then you are going to strongly over-emphasize a set of - presumably - speculative discussions about how an AI might behave, and if the training data came from reddit or stackoverflow that's probably going to weight-up patterns that were discussing The 3 Laws or morality or such which will produce banter (lots of civility, thank you, I'm pleased to help, etc).

The upshot of this is that it's really super hard to get some of the notebooks to do something very different than the specific scenario in the example - the arxiv web analysis example works less efficiently for other sites or other forms of processing of similar types of document, and begins to rapidly deteriorate in success rates as you move to more unrelated topics. Not unexpectedly, obviously, but it can drastically complicated learning the toolset. C.f ask it to search a short (2-4) list of rss or article feeds on news about ssds, gpus, or 3d printers in the last year to identify significant developments that have come to market to select factors/features worth looking for in choosing devices released in the last 6 months.

I would expect to see it struggle, perhaps, with extracting the data, or identifying "developments" - and depending on the LM used this does begin to surface, but mostly what happens - even with GPT 4 16k - is that it just starts to go a bit loopy or start just doing other things. A too-short prompt today regarding new TPUs resulted it in wanting to provide me with some surely deep insights into airline tickets.

If you eliminate the web search component, then results are obviously a factor of the model/settings/quality vs the alignment of key phrase or word patterns in the prompts with attention. I don't think most users realize that the difference between various prompt settings is sometimes just down to word positioning. "Do not create stub functions. Do not create empty methods." may result in attention on "do not create stub functions" and "create empty methods" whereas "Do not please create stub functions. Chicken* Do not create empty methods" may lead it to correctly attend to "[Do] not create empty methods" ('<Chicken><*>' being two arbitrary tokens) But because users instead make a change to, say, "Do not create stub functions and please do not create empty methods" it reinforces their perception that you are explaining or instructing the model rather than attention/pattern curating.

This is an incredibly easy mental trap to fall into while also trying to understand the effect of tweaking *code*.

Suggestion:
Standardize the setup portions of .py files in the notebooks directory so that each notebook can be more focused.

author: rickyloynd-microsoft

body:
Hi, @rickyloynd-microsoft,

Sure, the discussed concept explores augmenting Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-4 with advanced capabilities for logic and reasoning. This enhancement involves the LLM interacting with a range of texts—from philosophical works to scientific literature, and from legal documents to cross-disciplinary research. These texts are intended to provide rich contexts for responses, simulating improved reasoning skills for AutoGen.

An advanced approach involves integrating something like MemGPT for long-term memory and AutoGen for multi-agent collaboration. This setup would enable the LLM to access a set of general methods for hypothesis testing, evidence-based reasoning, and problem-solving. These methods would be stored as concise, labeled instructions in the LLM’s memory, allowing it to dynamically apply them to various tasks. This framework aims to allow AutoGen to mimic human-like problem-solving.

**Example 1:** For a legal analysis task, the LLM would retrieve and apply the 'Legal Documents and Case Law' text instruction set from its long-term memory. This would involve analyzing legal texts, interpreting legal language, and applying complex reasoning to deliver informed conclusions output by AutoGen.

**Example 2:** In a scientific research context, the model would use the 'Scientific Literature' text instruction set. It would engage in hypothesis formulation, data analysis, and evidence-based reasoning to contribute insights or solutions relevant to the scientific query at hand output by AutoGen.
author: Peter2023AI

body: Great ambitions. The hard parts are the details. What would you suggest as a first-step implementation to evaluate progress on this path?
author: rickyloynd-microsoft

body:
I completely agree: the challenging aspect lies in the details.

**Step 1:** This step could involve integrating essential components from MemGPT into AutoGen. This integration would enable AutoGen to perform function calls to long-term memory and search labeled reference documents. Access to long-term memory and reference documents is crucial, not only for humans but also for AI. When a person doesn’t know or remember how to do something, we seek out documents or other sources based on keywords under which the information might be labeled.

**Step 2:** A master section (labeled as such) must be added before any subsections. With every user request, the AI should read the master section in long-term memory for several reasons. Functioning like the Prefrontal Cortex of the human brain, the master section of the database will contain stored textual instructions guiding the AI on how to proceed based on the text prompt from the user or another AI. For instance, if the user or another AI prompts the AI to solve a “problem”, it will search the master section for a list of subsections labeled “problem”. If the information isn’t in the long-term memory database, the AI should resort to searching a document repository. If no information is found there, it could then search the internet using keywords or inform the user that more information is needed. The methodology for how, when, and why to search additional subsections, the document repository, the internet, or to ask the user for more information should not be hard-coded. Instead, it should be contained as independent, updatable text instructions within the master section and subsections. Wherever possible, the instructions and behavior of the AI system should be text/language driven, akin to how humans follow and enhance our understanding using an evidence-based process (refer to the following sub-processes) to determine when to make that decision.

**Step 3:** Once AutoGen can read, write, add, subtract, and update the label titles to data sections and data within those sections, it will be ready for Step 4.

**Step 4:** Develop a list of the most useful reusable processes. For instance, the processes I’ve listed could be improved, combined, or expanded to eliminate any possible redundancies before instructing the AI to populate them into the database. This could include sections for 1. Hypothesis Testing, 2. Evidence-Based Reasoning, 3. Logical Reasoning, 4. Problem-Solving Skills, 5. Inference from Limited Information, etc. Later, additional subsections could be added for more functions.

**Step 5:** Test and evaluate the results, making any necessary adjustments to the programming code. This structure would enable further improvements to be made almost entirely through text/language interaction. The AI(s) should follow streamlined text/language instructions for problem-solving, project management, and evidence evaluation, similar to the methods humans currently use based on stored text instructions in long-term memory or contained within documents.

**Step 6:** Later, the LLM itself could evaluate the information contained within the long-term memory database and document repository. Based on the weight of the evidence, it could make decisions on what to update within the LLM itself. This would allow for faster and more fluid changes between a given LLM and the long-term memory. Later, all the programming code could be converted to use the new https://www.modular.com/max/mojo.

body:
Analysis of AutoGen, Ollama, and Open-Source AI Frameworks
Current Situation

AutoGen has introduced a dependency on OpenAI in recent updates.
This change is causing issues for users who want to use purely open-source solutions like Ollama.
The integration of OpenAI into AutoGen raises concerns about Microsoft's influence and the true "openness" of the framework.

Potential Solutions and Their Implications
A. Drop AutoGen and Create Own Agents
Pros:

Complete control over the codebase
No unexpected dependencies
Can be tailored specifically for Ollama

Cons:

Significant development effort required
Potential loss of community support and updates
May need to recreate features already present in AutoGen

B. Find an Older Version of AutoGen
Pros:

Quick solution that allows continued use of AutoGen
Avoids OpenAI dependency

Cons:

Miss out on new features and bug fixes
Potential security risks from using outdated software
May become incompatible with other dependencies over time

C. Customize AutoGen from Source
Pros:

Retain AutoGen's core functionality while removing unwanted dependencies
Potential to contribute back to the open-source community

Cons:

Requires deep understanding of AutoGen's codebase
Ongoing maintenance effort to keep up with upstream changes
May create a fork that diverges significantly from the main project

D. Seek Alternative Open-Source Frameworks
Pros:

Potentially find a framework more aligned with open-source principles
Opportunity to explore newer, more flexible solutions

Cons:

Learning curve for new framework
Uncertain long-term support and development

Long-term Considerations

Open-Source Integrity: The incident highlights the importance of truly open-source solutions that don't have hidden dependencies on proprietary services.
Vendor Lock-in: Relying on frameworks tied to specific companies (like Microsoft) can lead to unexpected changes that don't align with users' needs or values.
Community-Driven Development: Supporting and contributing to genuinely open-source projects can help ensure that the AI community remains independent and diverse.
Transparency in Dependencies: Projects should be clear about their dependencies and the implications of those dependencies for users.
Modular Design: Frameworks that allow easy swapping of components (e.g., switching between different LLM backends) provide more flexibility and resilience against unwanted changes.

Recommended Long-term Strategy

Immediate Solution: Use an older version of AutoGen or create a custom fork that removes the OpenAI dependency. This allows continued development while a long-term solution is developed.
Mid-term Plan: Investigate alternative open-source frameworks or begin development of custom agents tailored specifically for Ollama integration.
Long-term Vision: Contribute to or initiate an open-source project that provides agent frameworks similar to AutoGen but with a strong commitment to open-source principles and flexible backend support.
Community Engagement: Raise awareness about the importance of truly open AI frameworks and gather support from like-minded developers and researchers.
Continuous Evaluation: Regularly assess the AI framework landscape to ensure that chosen solutions align with open-source values and technical requirements.

By taking these steps, you can work towards a solution that not only meets your immediate needs but also contributes to a more open and flexible AI development ecosystem.

One way to do that, i.e., intelligently figures out that it's time to ask for some human input, now is to use function call. You can write an `ask_human_expert` function, which just prints the current results and solicits human input, and let LLM decide when to use that function intelligently by registering the function to one or both agents.  Find a function call examples here: https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/main/notebook/agentchat_function_call.ipynb and https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/main/notebook/agentchat_two_users.ipynb.  There is an `ask_expert` function, which is conceptually similar to the suggested `ask_human_expert`, in the latter notebook.

Regarding the suggested solution:
The three-agent group chat solution is an interesting idea and presumably should work as well. It's worth trying.

For the support of intermediate value for human_input_mode between ALWAYS and NEVER: we have another supported value "[TERMINATE](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/main/autogen/agentchat/conversable_agent.py#L80)". It is still not that dynamic though. It is indeed potentially useful to support a more dynamic mode where LLM decides when to solicit human inputs. This requires revising the `check_termination_and_human_reply` function in the `ConversableAgent` class. 

@krishnashed let me know if what I said is clear to you, especially the function call idea. Thank you!

body:
Here is an example. I haven't tested but you can tune it from here.

```python

assistant = ConversableAgent(name="assistant", system_message=f"You are an AI assistant. You can ask for help from a human expert using the ask_human_expert function.")
user_proxy = UserProxyAgent(name="user proxy")

@assistant.register_for_llm(description="Function for asking human expert.")
@user_proxy.register_for_execution()
def ask_human_expert(question: Annotated[str, "The question you want to ask the human expert."]) -> Annotated[str, "Answer"]:
  answer = input(f"Please answer the question: {question}\n")
  return answer

user_proxy.initiate_chat(assistant, "Hey what is the age of the bedrock in grand canyon?")
```

Happy to give an example:

This are my agents (<name>: <description>)
* coder: has access to Neo4j and can answer analytical querries. Especially helpful if asked for trends, relationships and similiar
* press_observer: has full text access to articles of MediaX and MediaY, therefore can provide more context to answer questions that ask for reasons or detailed information. Not helpful to get trends.
* MediaX: can help with all questions regarding movies and actors as well as X and if user refers to "our" data.
* summarizer: Can create summaries of previous answers. Should talk as the last person, after all information to answer the question are already present in the conversation. Can not run functions!

Possible questions: 
* What are the most popular songs on Taylor Swift
* Which podcasts do we have on GPT-4
* What are the most recent News in the Israel Palestina Conflict

Task: 
For a question, I want to identify all agents that are relevant for this task. Then I want to send the question to each of those agents async, collect the answers, and evaluate if enough information is available to fulfill this task. If not, the agents should try to answer the question again, knowing what they tried before, but not taking care of messages from other agents. This process should be repeated until enough information is collected or a threshold is reached. Then finally, one agent (summarizer) should take all those information to provide a concise answer to the user questions.

body:
First of all, regarding the function not being available, it seems that the user proxy agent is in code execution mode not in function calling mode. I have seen this happen for Non-OpenAI models because they don't follow the OpenAI's function/tool call message format. So there is no `function_call` or `tool_call` field in the message from the model. Without those fields, user proxy agent cannot pick up the functions. Since you also mentioned the functions in the assistant's system message, the assistant produced code blocks in the message's `content` field. A code block triggers the user proxy agent into code execution mode, but the function definition is not in the code block, and that's why you see the error.

To make user proxy use the registered functions, the message from assistant must include a structured `function_call` or `tool_call` field following OpenAI schema.  One way to do that is to use structured generation through something like Guidance. 

Lastly, I you can use `register_for_llm` and `register_for_execution` decorators. They will make the code much simpler and you don't have to write any JSON schema. See: https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/docs/reference/agentchat/conversable_agent#register_for_llm

body:
1. Place your `run_compiler.sh` file in a working directory you have created.
2. Start you user proxy agent (assuming you are doing a one-on-one chat with an assistant agent) with the following setting:
```python
proxy = UserProxyAgent("user proxy", code_execution_config={"executor" : "commandline-local", "commandline-local": {"work_dir" : "your working directory path"}}, human_input_mode="ALWAYS") 

assistant = AssistantAgent("assistant", llm_config=..., system_message="<you need to tune your system message here, based on the default one but adding the instruction about how to use run_compiler.sh>")
```
3. Initiate chat
```python
proxy.initiate_chat(assistant, message="The task you want to do")
```

Oh, I forgot to mention, the command line code executor currently only supports Python. It takes a little work to make it support compiled-time languages -- by adding some additional handling for other languages. You can use the existing handling for Python as example.

body:
I think it is a good idea not to share any secrete with the executor because once a secret is in the executor's environment, it is accessible to LLM, which might be prompt-injected to leak your secret. So, if you really do share the secret with the executor, then there isn't difference between you sharing it directly via string or using environment variable. 

Instead, set up proxy servers alongside your application environment, and routing all authenticated traffic through the proxies.

Also, we currently are building new executors that can be more extendible. One example is a stateful IPython kernel executor so every code block is executed in a kernel -- no need for the LLM to rewrite the whole script each time. You can try it out using

```python
proxy = UserProxyAgent("proxy", code_executor_config={"executor": "ipython-embedded"})
```

You will need to update the Assistant Agent's system message to instruct it how to use the kernel executor. You can find an example prompt in `autogen.coding.embedded_ipython_executor.py`. 

--- Update ---

Alternative to code execution, you can also use the tool call feature, which is typically more secure because you restrict what kind of code gets run by providing LLMs with existing functions.

body:
For people still hitting this issue, especially those just trying to run this locally -- scroll down for the fix -- or read on for my ramblings of the issue: The actual problem is the default group chat admin -- It is hooked into the default gpt-4-xxxx-preview model. Even if you delete the model from the model tab, it's referenced -- and even hidden. It took me multiple times cycling through the UI to get it to appear. I had to then click the X on the model to unassign it. Since the gpt-4-1106-preview needs an openai key, it complains that the value is not set. I am someone who wanted to run this entirely local and never cared to set my OPENAI_API_KEY, and you don't need to. Beyond that, I also saw the gpt-4-1106-preview model on the primary_assistant agent, **even though I deleted and recreated it myself**, without giving it any models.

**Fix:** In short, any references to the gpt-4-1106-preview (or whatever model might be showing for your current version) need to be deleted. They might also be not showing up in the UI. The primary culprits are the default group_chat_manager and the primary_assistant. Especially the former, since you can't reassign that agent. Try to assign one of your local models to it, and the gpt-4-1106-preview should show up. X that out and save, and it should stop giving you the error. No environment variables need to be set, and you should be able to continue on fully locally. Naturally, if you want to use any hosted openai models, then you do need to set your API key.

The gpt model even had the audacity to show up on an agent that I created myself. There seems to be a bug that is auto-assigning that model (even when its deleted!) to agents without a model. So check all your agents. Better yet, delete and re-create, but make sure the gpt- models are never assigned. It seems the best method is to assign all agents a model, even if they don't need one. **If the error continues to come up in a group chat workflow, try and delete and recreate the buggy agent.** Last note, you need to recreate any existing workflows to get the errors to stop.

body:
**Solution for PowerShell Security Error in Windows:**

If you encounter a security error in PowerShell on Windows with the message:
```
+ CategoryInfo          : SecurityError: (:) [], PSSecurityException
+ FullyQualifiedErrorId : UnauthorizedAccess
```

and your execution policy is set to "Undefined," you can resolve it by granting unrestricted execution access to the process scope.

Here's the solution:

1. Open PowerShell as an administrator.

2. Run the following command:
   ```powershell
   Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process Unrestricted
   ```

   This command sets the execution policy for the current PowerShell session to "Unrestricted," allowing execution access without restrictions.

@crimson206 By following these steps, you authorize access to the code and resolve the security error.

body: This is a common source of confusion. When two agents are conversing, each maintains its own copy of the message history, and their roles are reversed in those two copies. The reason for this is because openai defined a fixed set of message roles like user and assistant, and autogen follows those roles in its message lists. In a group chat it may be that none of the agents represent the user, and yet every message list sent to the LLM must be annotated with user and assistant roles. The simple rule to remember is that every agent carries the assistant role in its own copy of the message list.

The main challenge of structured data is scale and schema understanding.

body: This is a common source of confusion. When two agents are conversing, each maintains its own copy of the message history, and their roles are reversed in those two copies. The reason for this is because openai defined a fixed set of message roles like user and assistant, and autogen follows those roles in its message lists. In a group chat it may be that none of the agents represent the user, and yet every message list sent to the LLM must be annotated with user and assistant roles. The simple rule to remember is that every agent carries the assistant role in its own copy of the message list.

Ugly but functional awaiting #1551. I have overridden the get_human_input method to support streaming with SocketIO. Additionally, I have set a global variable next_chat_trigger which is set to True when the LLM message ends with "COMPLETED", thus forcing an 'exit' and moving to the next sequential chat.

```python
    def get_human_input(self, prompt: str) -> str:
        global message_chat
        global next_chat_trigger
        
        if ( next_chat_trigger ):
            print('next_chat_trigger')
            next_chat_trigger = False
            message_chat = None
            return 'exit'
        else:
            socketio.emit('message', {"sender": agent_talking.name,
                    "content": prompt}, to = session['current_session_id'])

        while not message_chat:
            pass
        
        reply = message_chat
        message_chat = None

        self._human_input.append(reply)
        socketio.emit('message', {"sender": user.name,
                    "content": reply}, to = session['current_session_id'])
        
        return reply
        
```

author: maximedupre

body:
@maximedupre you raised interesting and important issue I haven't solved yet.

I think the best idea is to start simple. You can add to Engineer prompt few consice sentences that include most important infos about the project, for example: "Common styles placed in path/to/dir/..., don't create style locally when it available in common. File main.py intended to store endpoints only, any additional functions place in different files. Aplication log placed in something/log.txt, check it frequently and never overwrite.". Just keep it short to not distract LLMs attention, and it will be a good starting point for your agent.

If that approach will work for you, you can add next function for actualize that project summany when agent will learn something new about your project.

What about RAGs... well, it's a complicated topic. In my opinion in such case it has no sense to index whole your code base - better idea will be to write description of every file, what it contains and does, and index the descriptions. Then to provide path to the file in the metadata of the record, so you will be able to search appropriate files by description. But here will appear another problem - your agent will need to know what he actually wants to find. So in my opinion it's better to avoid RAGs, at least for beginning, and start simple.
