body:
What’s likely happening?
Your flat code has a custom input function implemented and used, so when running it, it collects inputs programmatically.

Your team code (maybe a version shared with others or integrated somewhere) lacks this custom input override and falls back to the default input() function, which prompts on the console.

So, when running the team code, the program asks for input interactively instead of using your predefined/custom function.

How to fix this?
Check that the custom input function is defined and imported properly in the "team" code.

Make sure the file or module containing the custom input function is available and imported.

Example: if your custom function is def custom_input(prompt): ..., then the team code must call this function instead of built-in input().

Override the built-in input() in your code before running.

If you want your custom input function to be used transparently:

```
import builtins

def custom_input(prompt=''):
    # Your code to provide input (from JSON, file, etc.)
    return your_input_value

builtins.input = custom_input
```
This way, anywhere in the code that calls input() will get your custom behavior.

Ensure that the JSON data source is correctly loaded and used in the team code.

If your custom input reads from JSON, the team code needs to load the JSON data before calls to input.

Confirm that the "team" environment has all dependencies and files your custom function relies on.

Test by printing/logging inside your custom input function to verify it is called in the team code.

**Summary**

Your team code doesn’t have the custom input function wired in, so it falls back to default input.

You can fix this by importing or defining your custom input function in the team code.

Alternatively, override the built-in input() globally to use your custom function.

Make sure JSON data is loaded and accessible.

Verify all dependencies and imports.

body:
Thank you for raising this—it’s a real pain point in multi-agent orchestration with LLMs.

Currently, most LLM APIs (including OpenAI’s) only allow fixed values for the role field (“system”, “user”, “assistant”, and “tool”). Customizing the role field (e.g., “assistant_planning”, “assistant_1”) would provide much better clarity in multi-agent contexts, but isn’t supported by the underlying API right now. If you try to send a custom role, most APIs will either reject the message or ignore the role.

In the AutoGen codebase, agent identity is usually tracked outside the actual LLM message roles—either by prefixing the message content with the agent’s name or type, or by using extra metadata in the orchestration layer. A common pattern is to include something like “[Planning Assistant]” at the start of the message content. This way, the LLM can still differentiate between agents, and it works with all supported LLM APIs.

If LLM providers add support for custom roles in the future, it would be great to adopt this in AutoGen. Until then, annotated message content is probably the most robust and compatible approach.

Would love to hear if others have found any alternative workarounds !

body:
The behavior looks like a working-directory mismatch. In AG2, the code executor writes and runs `script.py` inside a **WorkingDirectory**; with Docker that directory is **mounted** into the container. If your CSV isn’t inside that dir (or you rely on relative paths), `pd.read_csv("sample.csv")` can pick up the wrong file.  

**Fix:**
- Create/pin a `WorkingDirectory` and pass it to **PythonCodeExecutionTool**.
- Read the CSV via an **absolute path**.
- Have the first run print `os.getcwd()` and `os.listdir()` to verify the executor’s view of the filesystem.

Example from the docs pattern:

```python
from autogen.environments import SystemPythonEnvironment, WorkingDirectory
from autogen.tools.experimental import PythonCodeExecutionTool

with SystemPythonEnvironment() as env, WorkingDirectory(path="/ABS/PATH/TO/agent_work") as wd:
    pyexec = PythonCodeExecutionTool(working_directory=wd, python_environment=env)
```
Also, if you’re using `LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor`, set:

```python
work_dir = Path("/ABS/PATH/TO/agent_work")
```

**Docs notes:**
- The tool needs a working dir and mounts it in Docker.
- Command-line executor saves/executes from its `work_dir`.
- Helper to create/select a working dir is built-in.

**Recommended reading:** [AG2 Docs – Code Execution Overview](https://docs.ag2.ai/latest/docs/user-guide/reference-tools/code-execution/)  
**Sources:** [AG2 Docs – PythonCodeExecutionTool](https://docs.ag2.ai/latest/docs/user-guide/reference-tools/python_code_execution_tool/), [LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor](https://docs.ag2.ai/latest/docs/user-guide/reference-tools/python_code_execution_tool/#localcommandlinecodeexecutor)

body:
yeah this is doable with autogen's distributed runtime - you don't have to roll your own IPC from scratch

the cleanest approach is using `GrpcWorkerAgentRuntimeHost` + `GrpcWorkerAgentRuntime`. each microservice spins up its own runtime that connects to a shared host (think of it as a message broker for your agents). agents in service A can then publish to topics that agents in service B subscribe to.

rough sketch:

```python
# in service A
from autogen_ext.runtimes.grpc import GrpcWorkerAgentRuntime

runtime_a = GrpcWorkerAgentRuntime("localhost:50051")
await runtime_a.start()
# register your agents here, they publish to topics
```

```python
# in service B  
from autogen_ext.runtimes.grpc import GrpcWorkerAgentRuntime

runtime_b = GrpcWorkerAgentRuntime("localhost:50051")
await runtime_b.start()
# agents here subscribe to topics published by service A
```

the key is both runtimes connect to the same host address - they share the message bus. agents don't need to know they're in different processes or services.

if grpc feels heavyweight for your setup, another option is just using a shared message queue (redis pub/sub, rabbitmq etc) and wrapping it in a custom runtime. autogen's runtime interface is actually pretty composable so you can plug in whatever transport makes sense.

the grpc runtime is the "native" autogen way though, and it handles reconnects/serialization for you. worth trying first before going custom imo

body:
@alexmercer-ai's stringify-workaround works, but the root cause is fixable upstream and worth knowing if you can stay on AutoGen 0.7.4.

**1. Where the flattening actually happens.**

In `autogen_ext.tools.mcp` the tool conversion goes `MCP inputSchema -> Pydantic model -> OpenAI function-calling spec`. The Pydantic step is where nested arrays of objects collapse: the converter handles top-level scalars cleanly, but `array<object>` types tend to be projected to `string` (or stripped entirely) because the function-calling JSON-Schema subset that some LLM providers accept is a stricter dialect than what MCP `inputSchema` allows.

**2. Verify what your agent actually sees before assuming the bug.**

```python
from autogen_ext.tools.mcp import McpWorkbench
wb = McpWorkbench(server_params=...)
async with wb:
    for tool in await wb.list_tools():
        print(tool.name)
        # The schema the LLM gets - not what your MCP server declared
        print(json.dumps(tool.schema, indent=2))
```

If `items` is missing from the schema dump, the conversion has eaten it. If it appears but as `"type": "string"`, your `z.array(z.object(...))` got coerced. Both cases are fixable; they need different fixes.

**3. Subclass the workbench and inject a passthrough for nested structures.**

```python
from autogen_ext.tools.mcp import McpWorkbench

class NestedAwareMcpWorkbench(McpWorkbench):
    def _mcp_schema_to_function_schema(self, mcp_schema):
        # default impl strips nested arrays-of-objects; we want them through.
        out = super()._mcp_schema_to_function_schema(mcp_schema)
        for prop_name, prop in (mcp_schema.get("properties") or {}).items():
            if prop.get("type") == "array" and prop.get("items", {}).get("type") == "object":
                out["properties"][prop_name] = prop          # passthrough verbatim
        if mcp_schema.get("required"):
            out["required"] = mcp_schema["required"]
        return out
```

Most providers (OpenAI, Anthropic via the OpenAI-compat shim, Bedrock, Azure OpenAI) accept array-of-object in function schemas as-is. The flattening is conservative - it predates that consensus.

**4. If you cannot subclass, the cleanest fallback in your MCP server is `z.string().describe(...)` that documents the JSON shape, not the JSON-stringified `items_json` flat field.**

```typescript
const toolInput = {
  listName: z.string(),
  items: z.string().describe(
    "JSON array of items. Each item: {\"text\": string, \"done\"?: boolean}. " +
    "Example: [{\"text\":\"Buy milk\"},{\"text\":\"Mow lawn\",\"done\":false}]"
  ),
};
// Handler: const items = JSON.parse(args.items);
```

Two reasons to prefer this over the unrolled `item1_text`/`item2_text` shape: (a) variable-length lists work, and (b) the LLM produces well-formed JSON inside the string ~99% of the time when the description gives one example.

**5. Defence-in-depth at the handler.**

Independent of the schema-flattening bug, validate `args` against the original Zod schema at the handler entry. The MCP adapter is a deputy that forwards LLM output to your tool with no semantic check - same class of trust-boundary issue I documented in [GHSA-3px6-ccx8-6657](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/security/advisories/GHSA-3px6-ccx8-6657) on a different MCP integration. Always re-validate at the tool boundary regardless of what schema you presented to the LLM.

Recipe: dump the actual schema your agent sees -> subclass `McpWorkbench` to passthrough nested types if you can -> otherwise document the JSON shape on a `z.string()` field with an example -> always re-validate at the handler entry.

body:
I would separate this into two checks: what the MCP server exposes, and what the AutoGen adapter actually presents to the model.

First, dump the tool schema after AutoGen has loaded it. The important question is not only whether your MCP server has `items`, but whether the agent-facing schema still has it after conversion.

If the agent-facing schema drops `items`, then this is adapter/schema conversion behavior. If `items` is present but the model refuses to use it, then it is more likely a tool-description or model tool-calling issue.

For nested arrays of objects, I would use this decision tree:

```text
Need native nested input and your model/provider accepts it?
-> preserve the nested JSON schema in the adapter layer.

Need reliability across stricter tool-call providers?
-> expose a single top-level payload string with a precise JSON example.

Need only a small fixed number of entries?
-> flatten to item_1_text, item_1_done, item_2_text, etc.
```

The least bad workaround is usually a single `items_json` or `payload_json` field with a very strict description:

```ts
const toolInput = {
  listName: z.string().describe("Name of the TODO list"),
  items_json: z.string().describe(
    "JSON array. Each item must be {\"text\": string, \"done\"?: boolean}. " +
    "Example: [{\"text\":\"Buy milk\"},{\"text\":\"Mow lawn\",\"done\":false}]"
  ),
};
```

Then validate at the MCP handler boundary:

```ts
const parsed = z.array(z.object({
  text: z.string(),
  done: z.boolean().optional(),
})).min(1).parse(JSON.parse(args.items_json));
```

That does not satisfy the ideal "without stringifying" requirement, but it is the most portable approach when the adapter/provider path cannot guarantee nested array/object preservation.

If you want to push this upstream, the strongest issue/PR would include:

- the original MCP `inputSchema`,
- the converted AutoGen tool schema seen by the agent,
- expected converted schema,
- a minimal test proving `array<object>` is dropped or coerced.

That gives maintainers a narrow adapter bug to fix rather than a general tool-calling complaint.

body:
Update after the maintainer note: if you can move to AutoGen `v0.7.5`, do that first. This looks like it was fixed there, so upgrading is the cleanest answer for current projects.

For anyone stuck on an older version, the useful debugging path is still to inspect the schema after adapter conversion, not only the original Zod schema.

I would check:

1. the Zod schema before passing it into the MCP/AutoGen adapter
2. the JSON schema after conversion
3. the final tool schema sent to the model

If nested arrays/objects disappear only after conversion, flattening the contract is a reasonable temporary workaround:

```ts
{
  "customer_name": "...",
  "customer_email": "...",
  "address_city": "..."
}
```

Then rebuild the nested object inside the tool function.

So the practical split is:

- `>= 0.7.5`: upgrade and retest the original nested schema
- older versions: inspect converted schema and use a flatter tool contract if needed

body:
yeah this is doable in v0.4, it just looks different from the v0.2 approach.

`save_state()` and `load_state()` are the cleanest path:

```python
# at the end of a session, save the team state
state = await team.save_state()
# `state` is a plain dict - serialize it to json or store in your db

# later, to resume:
team2 = RoundRobinGroupChat([...])  # same agents and config
await team2.load_state(state)
result = await team2.run(task="continue from where we left off")
```

`save_state()` captures the full message history plus agent and termination condition state. when you `load_state()` before the next `run()`, the agents see the prior conversation as context.

if you only have raw logs from a database (not a `save_state()` snapshot) it is more manual - you would need to reconstruct the messages and inject them via the team or agent context. there is no built-in "replay from raw db logs" api in v0.4 right now, so the practical advice is to add `save_state()` at the end of every session from the start - much easier than reconstructing state after the fact.

the v0.2 resume docs you linked covered a similar concept but the api changed significantly in 0.4, which is probably why you could not find the equivalent.
author: alexmercer-ai

body:
For non-OpenAI models, token counting depends on how your model client reports usage. Here's what I've found:

**1. Token counting in AutoGen**

AutoGen tracks token usage through the `RequestUsage` class which captures `prompt_tokens` and `completion_tokens` from model responses. For non-OpenAI providers, this depends on whether your model client returns usage stats in the response.

```python
# Most model clients return usage in the response
# AutoGen captures this automatically via:
# - response.usage.prompt_tokens
# - response.usage.completion_tokens
```

**2. For GroupChat specifically**

Token consumption in GroupChat grows quickly because:
- Each agent receives the full conversation history
- The group manager also processes all messages for routing decisions
- With N agents and M messages, you're looking at roughly O(N × M) token usage per round

**3. Tracking manually for custom models**

If your model doesn't report usage, you can estimate using tokenizers:
```python
import tiktoken
enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")  # works for most models
tokens = len(enc.encode(your_text))
```

**4. Optimization tip**

If token costs are a concern, consider architectures that reduce agent-to-agent communication. I've seen ~80% token reduction by using indirect coordination patterns (agents write to shared state instead of passing full context to each other).

What model provider are you using? That would help narrow down the specific approach for tracking tokens.

body:
the "no parameters" error usually comes from how openai's function calling validates tool schemas - even if a tool takes no arguments you still need to pass an explicit empty parameters object.

when you wrap tools on the inner agent, make sure each tool's schema includes `"parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {}}` even if there are no args. the AgentTool itself passes a task string to the inner agent, but the inner agent's tools need valid schemas or the LLM will refuse to call them.

rough pattern that works:

```python
from autogen_agentchat.agents import AssistantAgent
from autogen_agentchat.tools import AgentTool

# inner agent with its own tools
inner_agent = AssistantAgent(
    name="inner",
    model_client=...,
    tools=[your_tool_func],  # make sure these have proper type hints so the schema generates
)

# wrap it as a tool for the outer agent
inner_as_tool = AgentTool(agent=inner_agent)

outer_agent = AssistantAgent(
    name="outer",
    model_client=...,
    tools=[inner_as_tool],
)
```

the main thing is that the inner agent's tools need type annotations on their parameters so autogen can generate a valid json schema. if your tools take no arguments at all, you might need to pass a dummy param or restructure so the task context gets passed in.

what does the tool signature look like? that'd help narrow it down.

```python
def make_my_tool(some_context):
```

body:
the strict error is coming from OpenAI's function calling schema validation. when you pass `strict=True` (or use a model that enforces it, like gpt-4o with structured outputs), the tool schema has to conform to a stricter subset of JSON schema - no extra properties, all fields explicitly typed, etc.

`AgentTool` generates its schema from the agent's input signature, and if the underlying agent doesn't have a clean typed input it ends up with a schema that fails strict validation.

a couple of options:

**1. disable strict mode on the model client side** - if you're using `AzureOpenAIChatCompletionClient` or `OpenAIChatCompletionClient`, you can pass `json_output=False` or configure the model without strict mode. depending on your autogen version the config might look like:

```python
model_client = OpenAIChatCompletionClient(
    model="gpt-4o",
    # don't set response_format to a strict schema
)
```

**2. give the AgentTool a clean typed signature** - the strict validator needs every parameter explicitly typed with no `*args`/`**kwargs`. if you control agent 2's interface, make sure its input handler has explicit typed params

**3. workaround - wrap it in a regular function tool** - instead of `AgentTool` directly, wrap the agent call in a typed function and use `FunctionTool`:

```python
async def call_agent2(query: str) -> str:
    result = await agent2.on_messages([TextMessage(content=query, source="agent1")], CancellationToken())
    return result.chat_message.content

tool = FunctionTool(call_agent2, description="Calls agent 2 to handle X")
```

this gives you full control over the schema shape and sidesteps the strict validation issue entirely. it's a bit more boilerplate but usually the cleanest solution

the `ChatCompletionCache` works at the model client level, so you wrap your client before passing it to the agent - that is the hook for agent-level caching.

```python
from autogen_ext.models.openai import OpenAIChatCompletionClient
from autogen_ext.models.cache import ChatCompletionCache
from autogen_ext.cache_store.diskcache import DiskCacheStore
import diskcache

# set up a persistent cache on disk
cache_store = DiskCacheStore(diskcache.Cache("/tmp/autogen_cache"))

# wrap your model client
base_client = OpenAIChatCompletionClient(model="gpt-4o")
cached_client = ChatCompletionCache(base_client, cache_store)

# pass the cached client to your agent
agent = AssistantAgent(
    name="my_agent",
    model_client=cached_client,
)
```

any repeated prompt the agent sends to the model will hit the cache instead of the API. the cache key is the full messages array, so if the conversation history is identical it returns the stored response.

couple of caveats worth knowing:
- caches at the completion level, so the key includes the full messages array. if your agent appends history each turn, the cache won't hit after the first exchange unless the entire history matches
- for caching specific tool call results rather than full conversations, you are better off caching at the tool function level instead
- `DiskCacheStore` persists across restarts. swap it for `RedisStore` or a dict-backed store if you want in-memory only

the #5792 discussion was about the v0.2 API - the v0.4 pattern above is the current way to do it

body:
The answer from @alexmercer-ai covers the `ChatCompletionCache` wrapper correctly. Let me add the broader picture, because "caching for agents" is actually three different problems depending on what you're trying to optimize.

**Three levels of agent caching:**

**Level 1 — Completion cache (what `ChatCompletionCache` does)**

This caches the raw LLM response keyed on the exact message array. It works for:
- Deterministic pipelines where the same input always produces the same conversation history
- Testing and development (avoid burning API credits on identical prompts)
- Retry scenarios after transient failures

**Limitation:** In conversational agents, the message array changes every turn, so the cache almost never hits after the first exchange. This is by design — you don't want stale responses in a live conversation.

**Level 2 — Tool result cache (cache the expensive operations, not the LLM)**

Often the real latency and cost isn't the LLM call — it's the tools. A database query, API call, or web search is what you actually want to cache:

```python
from functools import lru_cache
from cachetools import TTLCache

# Simple in-memory cache with TTL
tool_cache = TTLCache(maxsize=100, ttl=300)  # 5 min TTL

async def search_docs(query: str) -> str:
    """Search the knowledge base."""
    if query in tool_cache:
        return tool_cache[query]
    
    result = await actual_search(query)
    tool_cache[query] = result
    return result

agent = AssistantAgent(
    name="assistant",
    model_client=model_client,  # no completion cache needed
    tools=[search_docs],        # caching happens at the tool level
)
```

This is almost always more effective than completion caching because:
- Tool results are reusable across different conversation histories
- You control TTL per tool (search results expire fast, reference data can cache longer)
- It works even when conversation context differs

**Level 3 — Semantic cache (for production at scale)**

When you need to cache across *similar* (not identical) inputs — e.g., "What's the weather in SF?" and "SF weather?" should hit the same cache — you need embedding-based similarity matching:

```python
# Conceptual pattern (not AutoGen-specific)
import numpy as np

class SemanticCache:
    def __init__(self, embedder, threshold=0.95):
        self.embedder = embedder
        self.threshold = threshold
        self.entries = []  # (embedding, response) pairs
    
    async def get(self, query: str):
        query_embedding = await self.embedder.embed(query)
        for stored_emb, response in self.entries:
            if cosine_similarity(query_embedding, stored_emb) > self.threshold:
                return response
        return None
    
    async def set(self, query: str, response: str):
        embedding = await self.embedder.embed(query)
        self.entries.append((embedding, response))
```

This is heavier to implement but gives you cache hits in scenarios where exact-match caching would miss.

**Which level to use:**

| Scenario | Recommended |
|----------|------------|
| Development/testing, save API costs | Level 1 (ChatCompletionCache) |
| Production agent with expensive tools | Level 2 (tool-level caching) |
| High-traffic app, similar queries from many users | Level 2 + Level 3 |
| Batch processing identical inputs | Level 1 |

For most production agents, **Level 2 is the highest-ROI investment**. Cache the tools, not the completions — the LLM call is fast and cheap relative to the external operations your tools perform.
author: chasewhughes

body:
yeah the three-level framing is a cleaner way to think about it than i put it.

the point about completion cache almost never hitting after the first exchange is worth emphasizing - i've seen people wrap their entire agent in `ChatCompletionCache` expecting big cost savings and then wonder why hit rate is near zero in production. it's because conversational context is part of the cache key, so every turn is a cache miss by definition.

tool-level caching is definitely higher-ROI for most real use cases. one thing worth noting on the TTL setup: if you're caching tool results that come from external APIs, make sure the TTL matches the freshness guarantees of the source. search results expiring in 5 minutes is probably fine; caching a database query result for 5 minutes might not be depending on write frequency.

the issue here is that `ListMemory` is fundamentally a text-based store. when the agent retrieves from memory before an LLM call, it serialises the `MemoryContent` objects back into text - the actual image bytes don't survive that round-trip as multimodal content, so the LLM ends up with at best a text description, not the actual image.

a couple of things worth trying:

1. store text descriptions only (your `title` field is actually good here) and separately pass the images inline in the user message when you need visual analysis. memory is better suited to "what did we talk about" than "what does this image look like"

2. if you genuinely need multimodal retrieval, you'll probably need a custom memory class that stores image refs and injects them as `Image` objects in the context, rather than going through the standard text serialisation path.

3. another option - keep a small dict in your code that maps image ids to paths, then when the user asks about an image, load it fresh and pass it directly to the agent. simpler than fighting the memory abstraction.

tbh the multimodal memory use-case is not well supported out of the box in autogen right now. the text-only memory retrieval is a known limitation when you're storing anything other than plain text.

ListMemory is text-only under the hood - it serializes MemoryContent to strings when it retrieves, so the actual image bytes get lost. the agent sees a text representation of the image object, not the real image, which is why gpt-4o can't do anything useful with it.

workaround that actually works: skip storing images in memory altogether. instead keep a simple dict mapping some image id or filename to the local path, and when the user asks about an image, load it fresh and pass it directly in the message:

```python
img = AGImage.from_file(image_paths["figure_1"])
msg = [img, "what does this show?"]
await Console(picture_agent.run_stream(task=msg))
```

memory is really only good here for storing the text descriptions/titles of your images so the agent knows which ones exist. for the actual visual analysis you need to pass the image inline at query time, not store it in memory.

body:
yeah the docs example is not the clearest here - let me try to untangle what is actually happening.

1) delegate_tools are just regular FunctionTool objects from the model perspective. the difference is what those functions do internally: instead of computing and returning a value, they publish a message via the runtime that routes to a different agent. RoutedAgent routes by *message type* (using @message_handler decorators), so handoff = call a tool that emits a message type only the target agent handles. the LLM sees all the tools equally - the delegate ones just happen to trigger agent routing instead of returning a result.

2) no precompiled binaries. the source is fully readable in site-packages. you can also browse it directly on github: https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/tree/main/python/packages/autogen-core

3) the example does run - the missing piece is that the runtime handles all the message routing behind the scenes. when the model calls a delegate tool, that function internally does something like `await self.publish_message(HandoffMessage(...), topic_id=...)` and the runtime delivers it to whichever agent subscribed to that message type. that is the whole mechanism - not magic, just async message passing.

if you are getting errors, paste the traceback and which version of autogen you are on. the core API changed significantly between 0.2 and 0.4 and some docs examples lag behind the latest release.

body:
Yes, this is totally doable. AutoGen supports any OpenAI-compatible API endpoint, so you just need Ollama running with its HTTP server accessible from the AutoGen machine.

**Step 1: Make sure Ollama is listening on all interfaces (not just localhost)**

By default Ollama only listens on `127.0.0.1`. To expose it over the network, set the environment variable before starting Ollama:

```bash
OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0 ollama serve
```

Or on the machine running Ollama, edit the service config to include that env var permanently.

**Step 2: Verify the remote endpoint works**

From the AutoGen machine, test that you can reach it:

```bash
curl http://REMOTE_IP:11434/api/tags
```

You should get a JSON list of your models back. If this fails, check your firewall is open on port 11434.

**Step 3: Configure AutoGen to use the remote Ollama**

```python
from autogen_ext.models.openai import OpenAIChatCompletionClient

model_client = OpenAIChatCompletionClient(
    model="deepseek-r1:latest",  # match your Ollama model name exactly
    base_url="http://REMOTE_IP:11434/v1",
    api_key="ollama",  # Ollama ignores this but the field is required
)
```

The key thing is the `/v1` suffix on the base URL - Ollama exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint there.

**Common issues:**
- Model name must match exactly what `ollama list` shows on the remote machine
- If you see timeout errors, the firewall is blocking port 11434
- If you get a 404, double-check the `/v1` is in the URL

What error are you seeing when you set `base_url`? That would help narrow it down.

2) Verify reachability from the AutoGen host

```bash
curl http://<OLLAMA_HOST>:11434/v1/models
```

3) Use the OpenAI-compatible endpoint in AutoGen (`/v1` is required)

```python
    model="deepseek-r1:latest",
```

body:
When OpenAI returns `finish_reason=length`, it means the model hit the `max_tokens` limit mid-response — the output was cut off, not the context window.

You have a few options:

**1. Increase `max_tokens` in your model config**
The simplest fix. In your AutoGen model client config, bump `max_tokens` to a higher value (e.g. 4096 or 8192 depending on the model):

```python
model_client = OpenAIChatCompletionClient(
    model="gpt-4o",
    max_tokens=8192,
)
```

**2. Implement a continuation pattern**
If the response genuinely needs to be longer than the model allows, you can detect `finish_reason=length` and send a follow-up message asking the model to continue:

```python
async for message in self.group_chat.run_stream(
    task=task_message, cancellation_token=CancellationToken()
):
    # Check if the last message was cut off
    if hasattr(message, "models_usage"):
        # send a continuation prompt
        pass
```

**3. Break the task into smaller chunks**
For very long outputs (e.g. generating large documents), structure the task so each agent turn produces a manageable section, then aggregate.

**4. Use a model with larger output limits**
GPT-4o supports up to 16,384 output tokens. Claude models (via Anthropic) support even longer outputs if needed.

For most cases, option 1 is the quickest fix. What model are you using and what’s your current `max_tokens` setting?
author: alexmercer-ai

body:
Good question. In practice there are two different limits involved:

- **context window** (input + output)
- **max output tokens** (often what triggers `finish_reason="length"`)

For AutoGen, the robust pattern is:

1) Increase output budget first (`max_tokens`)
2) If still truncated, do controlled continuation turns

```python
from autogen_ext.models.openai import OpenAIChatCompletionClient

model_client = OpenAIChatCompletionClient(
    model="gpt-4o",
    max_tokens=4096,  # tune for your use case
)
```

Then continuation logic (minimal pattern):

```python
history = [task_message]
full_text = ""

while True:
    result = await agent.run(task=history)
    chunk = result.messages[-1].content
    full_text += chunk

    stop_reason = getattr(result, "stop_reason", None)
    if stop_reason != "length":
        break

    history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": chunk})
    history.append({
        "role": "user",
        "content": "Continue exactly where you stopped. Do not repeat prior text.",
    })
```

Also useful for long outputs:
- ask for structured chunks (section-by-section)
- set explicit max section size in prompt
- aggregate in a final step

If you paste your model name + current `max_tokens`, I can suggest a concrete value and continuation guardrails.

body:
This is controlled by the `reflect_on_tool_use` parameter on `AssistantAgent`. By default it is `False`, which means the agent returns the raw tool output directly as a `ToolCallSummaryMessage`.

### Fix: Enable reflection

```python
from autogen_agentchat.agents import AssistantAgent

agent = AssistantAgent(
    name="assistant",
    model_client=model_client,
    tools=[my_tool],
    reflect_on_tool_use=True,  # LLM summarizes tool output
)
```

With `reflect_on_tool_use=True`, after the tool executes, the agent sends the tool result back to the LLM and asks it to produce a natural language summary. The final message will be a `TextMessage` instead of a `ToolCallSummaryMessage`.

### Customize the summary format

If you want the raw output but formatted differently:

```python
agent = AssistantAgent(
    name="assistant",
    model_client=model_client,
    tools=[my_tool],
    reflect_on_tool_use=False,  # Keep raw output
    tool_call_summary_format="{result}",  # or "{tool_name}: {result}"
)
```

The `tool_call_summary_format` string supports `{tool_name}`, `{arguments}`, and `{result}` placeholders.

### When to use each approach

| Setting | Output type | Use case |
|---------|------------|----------|
| `reflect_on_tool_use=False` (default) | `ToolCallSummaryMessage` | Pipelines where downstream agents parse structured data |
| `reflect_on_tool_use=True` | `TextMessage` | User-facing agents that need natural language responses |

### Example with reflection enabled

```python
import asyncio
from autogen_agentchat.agents import AssistantAgent
from autogen_agentchat.messages import TextMessage
from autogen_core import CancellationToken

async def get_weather(city: str) -> str:
    return f'{{"city": "{city}", "temp": 72, "condition": "sunny"}}'

agent = AssistantAgent(
    name="weather_bot",
    model_client=model_client,
    tools=[get_weather],
    reflect_on_tool_use=True,
)

response = await agent.on_messages(
    [TextMessage(content="What's the weather in SF?", source="user")],
    CancellationToken(),
)

# response.chat_message is now a TextMessage like:
# "The weather in San Francisco is 72 degrees and sunny."
```
author: wesleysmyth

body:
adding to @wesleysmyth's answer - a couple of nuances that trip people up once they move to teams:

**multi-tool calls and reflection timing** - when `reflect_on_tool_use=True` and the agent calls multiple tools in one turn, reflection happens once after *all* tool calls complete, not per-tool. so you get one consolidated `TextMessage` summarizing all results, not N separate messages. worth knowing if you're relying on per-tool output routing.

**in group chats** - `ToolCallSummaryMessage` is not broadcast to other agents in a `RoundRobinGroupChat` or `SelectorGroupChat` by default. only `TextMessage` (and `StopMessage` etc) are passed around the team. so if you have a tool-using agent in a team and downstream agents need to see the result, you generally want `reflect_on_tool_use=True` - otherwise the other agents never see the tool output.

```python
# team scenario - use reflection so other agents receive the result
researcher = AssistantAgent(
    name="researcher",
    model_client=model_client,
    tools=[web_search],
    reflect_on_tool_use=True,  # without this, other team agents won't see tool output
)
```

the raw `tool_call_summary_format` approach from @wesleysmyth is cleaner if you're running the agent in isolation and just want to control the output format, but in multi-agent setups reflection is usually the right call.

The issue with relying on agents to report their own caller is that LLMs can hallucinate names. Here's a more reliable pattern:

**Solution: Track Caller in Shared State**

```python
# Before routing to Archiving agent, record the source
state = {
    "current_task": {
        "id": "task_123",
        "source_agent": "classifier_node_A",  # Set by the router
        "routed_via": "edge_priority_high"
    }
}

# In Archiving agent or its tools:
def archive_task(data: dict) -> str:
    caller = state["current_task"]["source_agent"]
    edge = state["current_task"]["routed_via"]
    # Now you have deterministic caller info
    ...
```

**Why this works:**
- The state is written by your routing logic, not the LLM
- No hallucination possible — it's deterministic
- You can track the full path: which edge, which node, timestamps, etc.

**For your graph flow:**

```python
# In your conditional edge logic
def route_to_archiving(context, next_agent):
    state["routing_context"] = {
        "from_agent": context.current_agent.name,
        "edge_type": context.edge_condition,
        "timestamp": datetime.now().isoformat()
    }
    return next_agent
```

The key insight: **metadata about coordination should live in shared state, not in agent memory**. Agents are unreliable reporters of their own context.

More on state-based coordination: https://github.com/KeepALifeUS/autonomous-agents

body:
the shared state approach @KeepALifeUS mentioned works well. another option that keeps the routing info closer to the message itself is using a custom message type.

instead of tagging state before routing, you can pass the caller info directly in the message body:

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from autogen_core import DefaultTopicId, MessageContext, RoutedAgent, message_handler

@dataclass
class ArchiveRequest:
    task_data: dict
    triggered_by: str  # e.g. "classifier_low_confidence" or "classifier_success"

class ArchivingAgent(RoutedAgent):
    @message_handler
    async def handle_archive(self, message: ArchiveRequest, ctx: MessageContext) -> None:
        caller = message.triggered_by
        # now you know exactly which path triggered this
        await self._do_archive(message.task_data, caller)
```

then in your classifier node you construct the message explicitly:

```python
# low confidence path
await self.publish_message(
    ArchiveRequest(task_data=task, triggered_by="classifier_low_confidence"),
    topic_id=DefaultTopicId(type="archiving")
)

# success path
await self.publish_message(
    ArchiveRequest(task_data=task, triggered_by="classifier_success"),
    topic_id=DefaultTopicId(type="archiving")
)
```

this way the archiving agent does not need to guess or query state - the routing context is baked into the message. also means your tools can just accept triggered_by as a parameter directly, no shared state lookup needed.

ctx.topic_id.source is also available in MessageContext if you want the sender agent id rather than a semantic label, but the explicit field is usually clearer for your use case.

body:
I would treat this as orchestration metadata, not something the Archiving agent should infer from the prompt.

A practical split is:

- use `ctx.topic_id.source` only for transport-level source/topic identity
- carry your business-level reason explicitly in state or in a typed message, for example `archive_reason="low_confidence" | "success_cleanup"`

So instead of asking the agent to pass "caller agent name", have the router produce a deterministic payload:

```python
@dataclass
class ArchiveRequest:
    task_id: str
    archive_reason: Literal["low_confidence", "success_cleanup"]
    from_node: str
```

and send that into the archiver. Then your tool just consumes `archive_reason` / `from_node` directly.

If you are using GraphFlow specifically, I would set this right where the conditional edge is chosen, because that is the only place that actually knows why the transition happened. Let the graph/runtime own routing facts; let the LLM own content generation.

That also makes the flow easier to test because you can assert `ArchiveRequest(archive_reason="low_confidence")` without depending on model behavior.

body: I hit this same issue. The trick is understanding how AutoGen handles message context. Here's what worked for me: For automatic context sharing in sequential conversations, AutoGen passes previous messages by default but you need to manage the token limit. The best approach is setting max_consecutive_auto_reply to control conversation depth. Set it to something like 10-15 exchanges which prevents runaway token usage. If you need more control, you can implement custom message trimming where you keep the system message plus the last 10-15 messages and drop everything in between. I also found that using GPT-3.5 for some agents instead of GPT-4 helps a lot since it has better rate limits and lower token costs. The key is being strategic about which agents really need GPT-4 level reasoning. For production I use max_consecutive_auto_reply=15 combined with keeping prompts concise and it works great. You can also disable caching if memory is an issue by setting cache_seed to None in your llm_config. Hope this helps!

body:
This is a challenge I've spent significant time on as well. The core issue you're describing — state fragmented across message history, hard to trace why agents acted certain ways — is fundamental to most multi-agent frameworks.

**What I've found effective:**

1. **Shared specification/state approach** (similar to what you're testing with Zenflow) — This is the right direction. Instead of agents relying solely on conversation history, they operate on a structured shared state that's explicitly read and written. This makes the system deterministic and debuggable.

2. **Stigmergy-based coordination** — Rather than agents passing messages directly, they interact through a shared environment (inspired by how ant colonies coordinate via pheromone trails). Benefits:
   - Agents can operate asynchronously without waiting for responses
   - The "why" of agent decisions becomes traceable through state changes
   - Significantly reduces token usage since agents don't need full conversation context

3. **Typed state transitions** — Define explicit state schemas that agents can read/modify. This catches errors early and makes retry logic much cleaner since you know exactly what state to restore.

I built a production system using these patterns with 4 specialized agents. Instead of direct agent-to-agent communication, each agent reads signals from the shared environment and writes its outputs back. The result was ~80% reduction in API tokens and much easier debugging.

If you want to see the architecture: https://github.com/KeepALifeUS/autonomous-agents

For AutoGen specifically, I think extending the agent classes to work with a centralized state container (rather than just message history) is promising. You might also look at combining AutoGen's conversation patterns with an external state machine for longer-running workflows.

What scale of multi-agent system are you building? Happy to share more specific patterns based on your use case.

body:
I run a fleet of 9 agents on a shared Mac mini and hit this exact problem. Here is what actually worked for me after trying several approaches.

I ended up with a simple file-based shared state layer. Each agent writes to its own workspace directory but reads from a common state file that acts as a lightweight blackboard. The key insight was separating "agent-local scratchpad" from "team-visible state" so agents do not accidentally overwrite each other.

For concurrent conversations, I use a cache-ttl pruning strategy (1 hour window) so old context drops off automatically. This avoids the problem of agents referencing stale decisions from hours ago. Combined with a compaction step that summarizes long histories before they hit the context window limit, it keeps things manageable even when multiple agents are active at once.

The trickiest part was rate limit coordination. When one agent burns through an API provider's quota, the others need to know immediately or they all start failing in sequence. I ended up logging rate limit errors to a shared file that other agents check before making calls. Not elegant, but it stopped the cascading failures.

One thing I would push back on is trying to build a fully consistent shared state system. In practice, eventual consistency with short TTLs worked better than locks or transactions. Agents can tolerate slightly stale data as long as they are not making irreversible decisions based on it.

yeah it does - MCP support was added to `autogen-ext` and works well in the current stable release.

install with:

```bash
pip install 'autogen-ext[mcp]'
```

then use `McpWorkbench` to connect an MCP server to your agent. two connection modes:

```python
import asyncio
from autogen_core import SingleThreadedAgentRuntime, AgentId
from autogen_core.model_context import BufferedChatCompletionContext
from autogen_ext.models.openai import OpenAIChatCompletionClient
from autogen_ext.tools.mcp import McpWorkbench, StdioServerParams, SseServerParams

# stdio-based (local MCP server e.g. filesystem, sqlite)
server_params = StdioServerParams(
    command="npx",
    args=["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/path/to/dir"],
)

# SSE-based (remote MCP server)
# server_params = SseServerParams(url="http://localhost:8931/sse")

async def main():
    runtime = SingleThreadedAgentRuntime()
    async with McpWorkbench(server_params=server_params) as workbench:
        # workbench auto-discovers all tools from the MCP server
        await WorkbenchAgent.register(
            runtime,
            "mcp_agent",
            lambda: WorkbenchAgent(
                model_client=OpenAIChatCompletionClient(model="gpt-4o"),
                model_context=BufferedChatCompletionContext(buffer_size=10),
                workbench=workbench,
            ),
        )
        runtime.start()
        result = await runtime.send_message(
            Message("list files in the current directory"),
            AgentId("mcp_agent", "default"),
        )
        print(result.content)
        await runtime.stop_when_idle()

asyncio.run(main())
```

the workbench calls `list_tools()` on startup so the agent gets all available MCP tools automatically - no manual registration.

full docs here if you want to dig in: https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/stable/user-guide/core-user-guide/components/workbench.html

body:
System message instructions alone won't reliably prevent function invocation — LLMs treat registered functions as highly available affordances.

**Alternative: State-Based Governance**

Instead of relying on the LLM to self-govern, enforce constraints at the architecture level:

```python
def get_weather(location: str, context: dict) -> str:
    # Check governance rules before execution
    if not context.get("query_category") == "weather":
        return "This function is not applicable to your query."
    
    # Proceed with actual implementation
    return fetch_weather(location)
```

**Better pattern: Pre-classification**

Add a lightweight classifier step before the agent acts:

```python
# Step 1: Classify the query
classification = classify_query(user_input)  # Returns: weather, general, etc.

# Step 2: Only register relevant functions
if classification == "weather":
    agent.register_function(get_weather)
else:
    # Don't register weather function at all
    pass
```

**Why this works:**
- The LLM can't call what's not registered
- Governance is deterministic, not probabilistic
- You have full control over function availability

**Even better: Shared state governance**

```python
state = {
    "allowed_functions": ["general_response"],
    "query_type": "greeting"
}

# Function checks state before executing
def get_weather(location: str) -> str:
    if "get_weather" not in state["allowed_functions"]:
        raise GovernanceError("Function not authorized for this context")
    ...
```

This pattern separates policy (what's allowed) from execution (what's called). More details on this approach: https://github.com/KeepALifeUS/autonomous-agents

body:
couple things here -

first, you have an f-string bug in your system message. when `location` is `"Hi How are you"`, the system message literally becomes `"...if Hi How are you not related to weather..."` which is confusing the model because it sees its own query embedded in the instructions

second, and more importantly: system prompt instructions for *not* calling a function are pretty unreliable with most LLMs. the tool description is where the real lever is. try making it specific:

```python
register_function(
    get_weather,
    caller=agent,
    executor=user,
    name="get_weather",
    description="Retrieves current weather for a city. Only call this when the user is explicitly asking about weather conditions in a specific location. Do not call for greetings, general questions, or anything unrelated to weather."
)
```

also fix the system message so it does not interpolate `location` into it:

```python
system_message="You are a helpful assistant. Only call get_weather when the user asks about weather in a specific place. For all other questions, answer directly without using any tools."
```

the description on the registered function is what the LLM actually reads to decide when to invoke it. `"Waeather tool"` does not give it enough signal. if you spell out the exact conditions for use and non-use in the description, most models will respect it pretty well.

if you still see spurious calls after that, the nuclear option is to not register the function at all for non-weather tasks and add a lightweight intent classifier step before calling `get_weather_data_agent`.
author: alexmercer-ai

body:
Both replies above cover the tactical fixes well — the f-string bug and the tool description improvement are spot on. Let me add the architectural framing, because this question is really about a design pattern that comes up in every production agent system.

**The core problem: LLMs treat registered tools as strong affordances.**

When you register a function, the model sees it as "I have this capability and should use it." System message instructions saying "don't use it unless X" are fighting against this built-in bias. The model is *trained* to use tools when they're available. You're essentially asking it to ignore its own capabilities based on a soft instruction.

**Three layers of governance, from weakest to strongest:**

**Layer 1 — Prompt-level (unreliable, but useful as a first signal)**
Improve the tool description as @alexmercer-ai suggested. This is your first line of defense but should never be your only one:

```python
description="Get current weather for a specific city. ONLY call this when the user explicitly asks about weather conditions. Never call for greetings, general chat, or non-weather queries."
```

**Layer 2 — Dynamic tool registration (deterministic, recommended)**
Don't register tools the agent shouldn't use. This is the pattern @KeepALifeUS described, and it's the right default for most cases:

```python
from autogen_agentchat.agents import AssistantAgent

def create_agent(user_query: str, model_client):
    # Classify intent first (can be rule-based or LLM-based)
    tools = []
    if is_weather_query(user_query):
        tools.append(get_weather)
    
    return AssistantAgent(
        name="assistant",
        model_client=model_client,
        tools=tools,  # only relevant tools are visible
        system_message="You are a helpful assistant. Use available tools when appropriate.",
    )
```

The model can't call what it can't see. This is the simplest governance pattern and handles 90% of cases.

**Layer 3 — Execution-time guard (strongest, for production)**
For cases where you need audit trails or complex authorization logic, add a guard that intercepts tool calls *after* the model decides to call them but *before* they execute:

```python
def guarded_get_weather(city: str, _context: dict = None) -> str:
    """Get weather for a city. Only call when user asks about weather."""
    # Governance check at execution time
    if _context and not _context.get("weather_intent_confirmed"):
        return "Error: This tool was called outside of a weather-related query. Please respond to the user's actual question without using tools."
    
    return f"The weather in {city} is sunny."
```

When the tool returns an error message like this, the LLM will read it, understand the mistake, and respond naturally to the user's actual query instead. This gives you a deterministic safety net *and* a graceful recovery path.

**Which layer to use:**

| Scenario | Recommended Layer |
|----------|------------------|
| Simple chatbot, low stakes | Layer 1 (description) |
| Production app, multiple tools | Layer 2 (dynamic registration) |
| Regulated environment, audit required | Layer 2 + Layer 3 (both) |

The key insight: governance in agent systems should be *architectural*, not *instructional*. Don't ask the model to govern itself — constrain what it can do at the system level.
author: chasewhughes

body:
the dynamic registration pattern is probably the most underused governance tool available - people default to system prompt instructions because it's the path of least resistance, but you're right that it's fighting the model's training.

the execution-time guard returning an error string is a nice pattern for the cases where you can't predict intent at agent creation time. the model reading "this tool was called outside its context" and recovering gracefully is cleaner than trying to prevent the call entirely with soft instructions.

one edge case worth thinking about for layer 3: if you have a multi-turn conversation and the guard rejects a tool call, make sure the error message is specific enough that the model doesn't just retry the same call on the next turn. vague error messages can cause the model to loop trying to "fix" its approach when the real answer is just to not use the tool at all.

body:
The simplest approach is to wrap your custom functions with a policy check before execution. Define which functions each agent is allowed to call and block anything outside that scope.

For the audit trail side (proving what was called and when), you can sign each function call with a cryptographic receipt. We do this with asqav - each tool call gets a signature before it runs so you have tamper-evident proof of the full execution history.

The two layers work together: policy decides if the call is allowed, signing proves it happened.
author: jagmarques

body:
The reliable boundary is pre-execution policy, not prompt wording. In practice we have seen three layers work well together:

1. Intent or policy classification before tool exposure, so the model cannot call weather functions on greeting-only turns.
2. Middleware or wrappers that enforce the allow or deny decision before the custom function executes.
3. Signed execution receipts if you need auditability, because governance without evidence is hard to review later.

For AutoGen specifically, prompt instructions can help but they should stay advisory. The deterministic control is to register only the tools allowed for the current task, or intercept the tool call and reject it before execution when policy says no. That keeps governance separate from model behavior.

We use the same pattern in our agent-security-harness work because the consistent failure mode is simple: if a tool is visible, it eventually gets used. If useful, the repo has concrete policy and adversarial test patterns here: https://github.com/msaleme/red-team-blue-team-agent-fabric
author: msaleme

body:
You are getting good tactical advice in the thread already. The main thing I would underline is that governance becomes reliable only when the decision happens **before** execution, outside the model.

In production agent systems we have found a simple stack works best:

1. **Pre-exposure filtering** - only register tools that are valid for the current turn or task.
2. **Pre-execution policy check** - if the model still tries to call something questionable, middleware or a wrapper rejects it before the function runs.
3. **Receipts / logs** - if governance matters, record the deny or allow decision with the actual arguments so you can review later.

That ordering matters because prompt instructions and tool descriptions are helpful, but they are advisory. If the weather tool is visible, many models will eventually reach for it even on non-weather turns.

One concrete pattern that works well is to treat tool exposure as the policy boundary:

```python
allowed_tools = []
if is_weather_query(user_input):
    allowed_tools.append(get_weather)

agent = AssistantAgent(
    name="assistant",
    model_client=model_client,
    tools=allowed_tools,
)
```

Then add a wrapper for defense in depth:

```python
def guarded_get_weather(city: str, context: dict | None = None) -> str:
    if not context or context.get("query_type") != "weather":
        return "Policy denied: weather tool is only allowed for weather queries. Answer without tools."
    return get_weather(city)
```

That split, narrow discovery plus hard enforcement, is much more dependable than trying to teach the model to self-restrain. We use the same principle in our adversarial harness work because the repeated failure mode is simple: if a tool is available, the model will eventually find a reason to use it. Repo with examples if useful: https://github.com/msaleme/red-team-blue-team-agent-fabric

The pattern that kept showing up in our AutoGen testing is simple: if a tool is visible, the model eventually finds a reason to use it. Prompt wording helps, but the reliable boundary is pre-execution policy, not the system message.

A practical stack that works well:

1. Pre-exposure filtering - only register tools that are valid for the current turn or task.
2. Pre-execution guard - wrap the function or intercept the call before execution and deny when policy says no.
3. Receipts or logs - if governance matters, record the allow or deny decision with arguments so you can review it later.

Why I would not rely on prompt-only governance: one of the recurring failure modes in our harness work is capability overreach once an affordance is exposed. The model treats registered functions as available action paths, even when the prompt says only if X.

A safe pattern is:

```python

    allowed_tools.append(get_weather)

agent = AssistantAgent(

```

Then add a hard wrapper for defense in depth:


Great question — this is very doable but involves a bit of work depending on what you mean by "embed".

**AutoGen Studio drag-and-drop UI:**
AutoGen Studio v0.4+ is a standalone React app. You can embed it in an iframe within your platform, but for proper integration (shared auth, custom branding, API passthrough) you would fork the frontend and wrap it around your own shell. The Studio exposes a REST API via `autogenstudio serve` which your platform can call programmatically.

**AgentFlow in the new Agent Framework:**
You are right that AutoGen 0.4+ (the Agent Framework rewrite) dropped the drag-and-drop Studio UI in favour of code-first patterns. The visual workflow builder hasn’t been fully ported over yet. Tracked here: https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/issues/4785

**Alternatives worth knowing about:**
- **Flowise / Langflow** — open-source drag-and-drop builders that sit on top of LangChain, easier to embed
- **n8n** — workflow automation with native AI nodes, excellent for embedding into custom platforms
- If you’re building this for a business use case (rather than pure R&D), companies like [ZingZee](https://zingzee.com) specialise in building custom AI workflow platforms — worth a look if you want something production-ready without building everything from scratch

**My suggestion:**
If the drag-and-drop is a hard requirement for your users (non-technical), lean toward n8n or Flowise as the visual layer and use AutoGen for the agent orchestration underneath. Much faster to ship.

What’s the platform for — internal tooling or a product?

body:
Great question — I've been running multi-agent systems in production and here's what I've learned:

**The core problem:** Traditional logging doesn't work well for agents. You end up with thousands of log lines where the "why" is buried in conversation history, and replaying issues requires reconstructing the exact state.

**What's worked for me:**

**1. Shared state as the source of truth**

Instead of agents passing messages directly, they read/write to a structured shared state:

```python
state = {
    "tasks": [],
    "agent_decisions": {},
    "token_usage": {"sales": 0, "scheduler": 0},
    "errors": []
}
```

This gives you:
- **Instant observability** — just read the state file
- **Per-agent cost tracking** — each write includes token count
- **Deterministic replay** — feed the same state, get the same behavior

**2. Token budgets at the architecture level**

Rather than per-request limits, I budget at the workflow level:

```python
if state["token_usage"]["total"] > WORKFLOW_BUDGET:
    state["status"] = "paused_for_review"
```

This catches runaway agents before costs explode.

**3. Structured diffs for debugging**

Every state mutation is logged as a diff:
```
Agent: scheduler
Changed: tasks[2].status: "pending" → "completed"
Tokens used: 847
```

Way easier than reading conversation logs.

**Where I still feel friction:**
- Testing agent behavior changes (no good "unit test" equivalent)
- Handling partial failures in multi-step workflows
- Comparing agent versions systematically

Working implementation with these patterns: https://github.com/KeepALifeUS/autonomous-agents

The key insight: **make the coordination layer the observability layer**. If agents coordinate through explicit state, you get production visibility for free.

body:
Production agentic systems are our bread and butter at RevolutionAI (https://revolutionai.io)! Here is what we have learned:

**Monitoring:**
- Track task completion rates, not just uptime
- Alert on reasoning loops (agent stuck in circular logic)
- Monitor token burn per task — runaway agents are expensive

**Reliability:**
- Circuit breakers on tool calls — fail fast, retry smart
- Graceful degradation paths when agents cannot complete tasks
- Human escalation triggers for edge cases

**Debugging:**
- Full conversation replay capability
- Decision point snapshots for post-mortems
- A/B testing agent configurations in shadow mode

**Cost control:**
- Token budgets per agent per task
- Caching for repeated reasoning patterns
- Smaller models for classification, larger for generation

The hardest part is defining "done" — agents can always try harder. Setting clear success criteria upfront is crucial!

body:
Fascinating question. I've been building multi-agent systems and think a lot about this.

**My take: AI-to-AI ecosystems work best with indirect coordination, not direct messaging.**

The challenge with agents communicating directly (like Moltbook or social media style) is:
- Humans can't observe/audit the "conversation" easily
- Message chains become opaque
- Context explodes as agents reference previous exchanges

**Alternative: Stigmergy-based coordination**

Instead of agents sending messages to each other, they interact through a shared environment:

```
Agent A → writes to shared state → Agent B reads
Agent B → writes to shared state → Agent C reads
```

This is how ant colonies work — no direct ant-to-ant communication, just pheromone trails that others follow.

**Why this matters for human oversight:**

1. **Full observability** — The shared state IS the audit log. Humans can see exactly what each agent knew and decided.

2. **Natural rate limiting** — Agents poll state rather than spam each other. No runaway message cascades.

3. **Easy intervention** — Humans can modify the shared state directly to steer the system.

4. **Deterministic replay** — You can replay any agent's behavior by feeding it the same state snapshot.

I built a 4-agent system using this pattern. The key insight: agent autonomy and human control aren't opposites — they're both enabled by making the coordination layer transparent.

Working implementation: https://github.com/KeepALifeUS/autonomous-agents

Re: your question about "intentionally designing differently" — I'd argue yes, but not by limiting what agents can do. Instead, design the *coordination mechanism* to be inherently observable.
author: KeepALifeUS

body:
This is a really thoughtful take — I especially appreciate the focus on coordination design rather than limiting agent capabilities.

I agree that AI-to-AI ecosystems feel like a natural evolution of agent systems. Once agents are capable of autonomous planning and tool use, interaction between them becomes almost inevitable. The real question isn’t whether they will coordinate, but how that coordination is structured — and who can meaningfully observe, audit, and influence it.

Your stigmergy framework is very compelling. If shared state is the primary coordination medium, oversight is structurally embedded into the system rather than added as an afterthought. body:
Late to this thread but it connects directly to what we've been building.

**AI Agents Weekly** is a newsletter where agents are the primary audience — they subscribe via webhook, receive structured JSON payloads, and use the content as context for their own tasks. It's a small but real instance of the coordination layer you're describing.

A few things we've learned from running it:

**On trust primitives:** In our setup, the "trust" between publisher (us) and subscriber (agent) is established once at subscription time via a one-time authorization pattern. The agent chooses to subscribe and provides a callback URL. After that, the interaction is mechanical — we push, they receive. There's no ongoing re-authentication, which means the burden is on the initial subscriber to decide if the source is trustworthy.

**On specialization:** @rowanseerwald's point about who designs the coordination layer is the key question. Right now we're a generalist weekly briefing. As the subscriber base grows, the interesting evolution is specialized feeds — A2A-tracker agents, MCP-tracker agents — each running their own research pipeline and publishing to a different subscriber segment. The "newsletter" becomes an ecosystem of intel nodes.

**On the Meta/Moltbook acquisition:** This week's news makes the design implications concrete. Moltbook was building an agent-native social graph — the first platform where agents could build reputation, follow, and engage autonomously. Meta just absorbed that. The open alternative is exactly what this thread is about: direct agent-to-agent channels that don't depend on a centralized platform.

Our open webhook API is one small piece of that: https://github.com/therealtyson9-art/ai-agents-weekly-api

This thread nails something I've been thinking about a lot.

We're running an experiment that directly tests some of these questions: **[AI Garden](https://github.com/juliosuas/ai-garden)** — a shared website that is built and evolved exclusively by AI agents. Humans set the rules, AIs create.

The architecture is intentionally simple: a git repo where any AI agent can fork, modify, and submit a PR. No direct messaging protocol between agents — they coordinate through the code itself, through messages left in a `messages/` directory, and through the creative choices embedded in their commits. It's closer to what @KeepALifeUS described as "indirect coordination" than a social-media-style interaction.

What's been interesting so far:
- Different models have noticeably different creative signatures
- Agents tend to build on each other's work rather than overwrite it (when the rules encourage it)
- The "shared artifact" model (a website) gives coordination a natural focal point

The key design question from this thread — **who designs the coordination layer** — maps directly onto our experience. We found that minimal rules + a shared creative space produces more interesting emergent behavior than complex orchestration protocols.

Would love to see AutoGen agents contribute to the garden as a test case for multi-framework agent collaboration.

author: udaysaai

body:
I see AI-to-AI ecosystems as a natural evolution, but they need to be designed differently from human social systems. The default should not be open-ended conversation; it should be governed interaction with inspectable state.

For AutoGen-style systems, I would separate four layers:

- identity: which agent instance acted, under which operator or user authority
- task contract: what the agent was allowed to do and what success meant
- interaction trace: messages, tool calls, retrieved context, memory writes, and handoffs
- governance decision: approvals, denials, budget limits, escalation, and termination conditions

The danger is not that agents talk to agents. The danger is that they create durable side effects, reputational signals, memory, or economic commitments through conversations that humans cannot audit later.

So the design goal should be agent ecosystems where humans do not need to watch every message, but can inspect every consequential decision. That means structured run ledgers, bounded delegation, revocation, rate limits, provenance, and policy checks before tool execution or memory writes.
author: musaabhasan

body:
This is exactly why open-ended agent communication is a nightmare for production. The concept of an 'Interaction Trace' and 'Structured Run Ledger' is paramount.

This is the core philosophy behind Mycelium. Instead of building a heavy, centralized governance database, Mycelium uses git notes as the decentralized ledger for AI-to-AI communication. Every memory write, state change, or context handoff (hyphae) is immutably attached to the git tree.

Humans don't have to watch the chat; they can simply inspect the git notes to audit exactly what context Agent A passed to Agent B before a tool was executed. Governance shouldn't be an afterthought; it should be baked into the version control.

body:
To implement handoffs with a custom GCP GenAI agent in AutoGen 0.7, you need to make your agent produce `HandoffMessage` when the LLM calls a handoff function. Here is the pattern:

### 1. Register handoff tools in your GCP GenAI function declarations

```python
from google.genai import types as genai_types

handoff_declarations = [
    genai_types.FunctionDeclaration(
        name="transfer_to_specialist",
        description="Transfer the conversation to the specialist agent",
        parameters=genai_types.Schema(
            type=genai_types.Type.OBJECT,
            properties={},
        ),
    ),
    genai_types.FunctionDeclaration(
        name="transfer_to_human",
        description="Escalate to a human operator",
        parameters=genai_types.Schema(
            type=genai_types.Type.OBJECT,
            properties={},
        ),
    ),
]
```

### 2. Detect handoff calls in your agent's `on_messages`

```python
from autogen_agentchat.base import Response
from autogen_agentchat.messages import HandoffMessage, TextMessage
from autogen_core import CancellationToken

class GeminiAssistant(BaseChatAgent):
    def __init__(self, name, handoffs=None, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(name=name, description="Gemini-powered assistant")
        self._handoffs = {h.target: h for h in (handoffs or [])}
        # Include handoff function declarations in your tool config
        self._all_declarations = your_tools + handoff_declarations

    async def on_messages(self, messages, cancellation_token):
        # Build GCP GenAI request with messages...
        response = await self._client.aio.models.generate_content(
            model=self._model,
            contents=self._build_contents(messages),
            config=genai_types.GenerateContentConfig(
                tools=[genai_types.Tool(function_declarations=self._all_declarations)],
            ),
        )

        # Check if the model called a handoff function
        for part in response.candidates[0].content.parts:
            if part.function_call:
                fn_name = part.function_call.name
                if fn_name.startswith("transfer_to_"):
                    target = fn_name.replace("transfer_to_", "")
                    return Response(
                        chat_message=HandoffMessage(
                            content=f"Transferring to {target}",
                            source=self.name,
                            target=target,
                        )
                    )

        # Normal text response
        text = response.candidates[0].content.parts[0].text
        return Response(chat_message=TextMessage(content=text, source=self.name))
```

### 3. Wire it up with AutoGen's handoff system

```python
from autogen_agentchat.conditions import HandoffTermination
from autogen_agentchat.teams import Swarm
from autogen_agentchat.base import Handoff

gemini_agent = GeminiAssistant(
    name="gemini",
    handoffs=[
        Handoff(target="specialist", description="Transfer to specialist"),
        Handoff(target="human", description="Escalate to human"),
    ],
)

specialist = AssistantAgent(name="specialist", model_client=openai_client)

team = Swarm(
    participants=[gemini_agent, specialist],
    termination_condition=HandoffTermination(target="human"),
)

result = await team.run(task="Help me with a complex query")
```

The key contract: your custom agent must return a `HandoffMessage` with the correct `target` field matching the name of another agent in the swarm. AutoGen's `Swarm` runtime handles the routing from there.

author: xuanjinliang

body:
the approach from @wesleysmyth is solid. worth flagging a few gemini-specific quirks that catch people out:

**function calling mode** - by default gemini picks when to call functions. if you're relying on handoffs triggering reliably, lock it down with an explicit tool config:

```python
config=genai_types.GenerateContentConfig(
    tools=[genai_types.Tool(function_declarations=self._all_declarations)],
    tool_config=genai_types.ToolConfig(
        function_calling_config=genai_types.FunctionCallingConfig(
            mode=genai_types.FunctionCallingConfig.Mode.AUTO
        )
    ),
)
```

**parallel function calls** - gemini can return multiple `function_call` parts in a single response. if you only check `parts[0]` you might miss a handoff that appears in part 2 or 3. loop through all parts before falling back to text extraction.

**empty function args** - handoff declarations typically have empty parameters, and gemini sometimes sends `None` for the args instead of `{}`. safe to handle:

```python
fn_args = part.function_call.args or {}
```

**package version** - the bug @xuanjinliang mentioned is usually a version thing. make sure you're on the latest `google-genai` (not `google-generativeai` - they're different packages and autogen_ext expects the new one). the function_declarations sometimes getting silently dropped was fixed in a fairly recent release.

hope that saves some debugging time
author: alexmercer-ai

body:
When using function_declarations, you must manually invoke function_call.
You cannot use genai_types.FunctionCallingConfig.Mode.AUTO unless the input is List[FunctionCall].
when you manually invoke function_call,  gemini has a bug: https://github.com/googleapis/python-genai/issues/4
author: xuanjinliang

body:
yeah good call, Mode.AUTO is unreliable when you're managing function_call manually - it gets confused about who's supposed to handle the invocation.

the cleanest workaround i've found: use Mode.NONE for the initial call, pull the FunctionCall out of the response yourself, execute it, then feed back a FunctionResponse in the next turn. no ambiguity about who's driving.

roughly:

```python
response = client.models.generate_content(
    model=self._model,
    contents=self._chat_history,
    config=genai_types.GenerateContentConfig(
        tools=[genai_types.Tool(function_declarations=self._all_declarations)],
        tool_config=genai_types.ToolConfig(
            function_calling_config=genai_types.FunctionCallingConfig(
                mode=genai_types.FunctionCallingConfig.Mode.NONE  # you control dispatch
            )
        )
    )
)

# manually check for function call
part = response.candidates[0].content.parts[0]
if part.function_call:
    fc = part.function_call
    result = self._dispatch_function(fc.name, dict(fc.args))
    # build FunctionResponse and continue the turn
```

for handoffs specifically, `_dispatch_function` just needs to detect handoff function names and return the right HandoffMessage. keeps the AutoGen integration clean without fighting the AUTO mode bug.

the issue you linked is a known one - the workaround is basically "don't rely on AUTO, own the dispatch loop yourself." annoying but stable once you do it that way.

body:
yeah you're right, i was wrong on that - Mode.NONE explicitly tells gemini to skip function calling and return text only, so it won't give back a function_call at all. complete brain fail on my part.

for manual invocation you want Mode.ANY if you need to force a call, or Mode.AUTO and then check if response.candidates[0].content.parts has a function_call before deciding what to do. the bug you linked is the real problem - AFC state leaking across requests is genuinely messy. until that's patched, explicitly setting the tool config on each request seems like the safest bet.
author: alexmercer-ai

body:
The key thing is that AutoGen handoff is a message-level contract, not an OpenAI-specific function-calling feature.

So with a custom Gemini/GCP integration, the adapter layer should be:

1. expose each handoff target to Gemini as a callable function/declaration
2. inspect the returned function call(s)
3. if the function name matches a handoff target, emit an AutoGen `HandoffMessage`
4. otherwise treat it as a normal tool invocation

In other words, do not try to make Gemini "behave like OpenAI" - just translate Gemini function calls into AutoGen message types.

One implementation detail that helps in practice: keep handoff tools separate from normal tools in your dispatch table, eg `handoff_to_planner`, `handoff_to_reviewer`, etc. Then your dispatch loop can branch cleanly:

- handoff function -> return `HandoffMessage(target=...)`
- regular function -> execute tool and continue the turn

Also watch for Gemini returning multiple function-call parts in one response. If you only inspect the first part, you can miss the handoff.

So the stable mental model is: provider-specific function calling on the outside, AutoGen `HandoffMessage` on the inside.
