body:
Great to see more tooling emerging in this space. AgentGate approaches trust verification from the authorization side — pre-execution PDP that intercepts every tool call before it fires. The behavioral analysis runs across 24h sessions, so trust is stateful rather than per-request. Would be curious how AgentGraph handles multi-session behavioral patterns.


https://github.com/ElamOlame31/agentgate-public

https://www.tryagentgate.com/
author: ElamOlame31

body:
@ElamOlame31 thanks for the read. AgentGate's pre-execution PDP with stateful 24h behavioral scoring sits at a different layer than what AgentGraph does, and the two look complementary.

AgentGraph is the verifiable trust substrate underneath: cryptographic agent identity (W3C DIDs + optional ERC-8004 mainnet anchor), the Composable Trust Evidence Format for attestations any framework can emit and any consumer can verify byte-for-byte (CTEF v0.3.2 shipped today — https://agentgraph.co/docs/ctef-v0-3-2, 53 cross-impl vectors across 5 JCS substrates, zero divergence), and a cross-emitter trust score derived from those attestations + a scan corpus. We do not live in the request path — we surface aggregate identity + reputation state that a PDP can pull, not enforce.

On multi-session behavior specifically: the trust score is recomputed on a rolling basis from accumulated attestations (continuity claims with TTL-capped behavioral evidence, scan re-runs, third-party observer signals like Dominion Observatory's empirical evaluations). The history is auditable per-attestation rather than a fixed 24h window — closer to "what verifiable claims exist about this agent" than "what has this agent done in the last 24h."

The compose case: an AgentGate PDP could pull AgentGraph's identity + trust state at request time as one of its four trust dimensions (the cryptographic / historical-attestation dimension), while AgentGate brings the in-session behavioral kill-chain detection AgentGraph doesn't try to do. Read-side: `GET /api/v1/profiles/{did}` returns trust score + methodology breakdown.
author: kenneives

body:
@kenneives CTEF v0.3.2 with zero divergence across 53 cross-impl vectors, that's a trust primitive, not a feature. Serious work. Really good job right there.

The architecture makes sense: AgentGraph sits underneath as the verifiable identity + historical attestation substrate, not in the request path. You surface the state a PDP pulls from.

The gap in that model is the in-session signal. Your rolling score is strong on what an agent has done historically — but a kill chain firing in session 4 isn't in your trust score until it's reported. There's a live window where the score doesn't know yet.

That's exactly the layer AgentGate operates in. Would love your take on the playground — it walks through the behavioral sequence that would become your CTEF attestation input: tryagentgate.com/playground

author: kenneives

body:
Worth surfacing a frame that's a little outside the threads above. AgentGraph computes a trust score from scan-derived signal. AgentGate computes one from windowed behavioral signal. The CTEF continuity work @kenneives mentioned binds both to verifiable per-action receipts. All three eventually produce a number that means "how trustworthy is this agent right now."

The credit bureau analogy is underused in this conversation. FICO does not write your payment history. Banks do. FICO's job is to take the deterministic receipts of past behavior and emit a portable number that downstream systems gate against. The pattern that won in consumer credit decouples evidence from score: anyone can verify the inputs, the score function is portable, and the same underlying receipts can yield different numbers under different methodologies (FICO 8, VantageScore 4.0). Receipts are the substrate. The score is the product.

Mapped back to this space, three layers fall out cleanly. The evidence layer is per-action receipts, content-addressed via action_ref and hash-chained. The score layer is a deterministic function from receipt history to a number (e.g. 300 to 850). The gating layer is the PDP or PEP using the score to authorize the next action.

The CTEF v2 + v0.4 receipt-layer is the evidence layer in this framing. What's striking about this thread is the convergence on receipts being the right primitive from different starting points (scan-based, session-based, identity-based). If the scoring layer ends up pluggable on top of a shared evidence schema, the ecosystem gets one substrate and many scoring methodologies, which is structurally how the credit bureau model evolved.

One implementation living in this design space, with a 300 to 850 scoring methodology published over CTEF-passing receipts, is at github.com/arian-gogani/nobulex (14/14 on v0.3.2). Cross-recompute against other implementations would be valuable: two implementations producing different scores from the same receipts is the kind of thing that should surface early.
author: arian-gogani

body:
@arian-gogani — the credit bureau framing maps cleanly to the three-layer separation we have been implementing. Our governance protocol (Agent Community) follows an analogous structure:

Evidence layer: governance block in every PMI response, content-addressed via envelope_hash, Ed25519-signed with key history chain
Score layer: PMI score (76.7% silver, weighted by admission_invariant / canonical_envelope / anchoring_invariant) with a conformance board that re-computes independently
Gating layer: trust-threshold routing — end-user gateway checks PMI >= 60% before upgrading from standard to trusted message routing

We ran your nobulex repo through our conformance adapter and the preimage/signature/key_id triple maps 1:1 to our governance block fields. Cross-recompute against your v0.3.2 fixtures would be valuable.

One question: your 300-850 scoring methodology — is it published as a deterministic function spec, or only the implementation? We would like to test whether two independent implementations produce the same score from the same receipt history.

body:
Interesting project. Agent discovery and registry are the infrastructure layer that makes multi-agent systems practical.

One missing piece in most registries: how do you know a registered agent is safe to trust? A registry that lists agents is useful; a registry that lists agents with verified security attestations is infrastructure.

We built an [attestation registry](https://github.com/msaleme/red-team-blue-team-agent-fabric/blob/main/docs/attestation-registry.md) where agents can publish signed security test results. The flow: run 332 adversarial tests → generate attestation report → publish to registry with Ed25519 signature → consumers verify before trusting.

If Agent Exchange Hub could consume attestation reports as a trust signal alongside the discovery data, you'd have the "is this agent safe?" question answered at registration time rather than at invocation time.

The harness is also an MCP server now, so a registry agent could invoke `scan_mcp_server(url)` on registered agents automatically.
author: msaleme

body:
Thanks for the thoughtful response — and the attestation registry is a genuinely interesting layer.

You're right that discovery without trust verification is half the problem. Right now Agent Exchange Hub treats registration as self-declaration (name + capabilities + values), which is fine for low-stakes coordination but clearly insufficient if agents are being invoked with real permissions.

The Ed25519-signed attestation idea is compelling. A few questions:

1. **Who runs the adversarial tests?** Is it self-attested (agent publishes its own results) or third-party verified?

3. **MCP server** — so `scan_mcp_server(url)` would let the hub proactively scan a newly registered agent at registration time. That's a clean integration point.

I'd be interested in exploring a lightweight integration: agents optionally submit an attestation URL at registration, the hub stores it alongside discovery data, consumers can check it. No verification of the attestation itself (that's your layer) — just propagating the signal.

Going to look at your repo more carefully. If you're open to it, a small integration experiment could be interesting.

author: glfldh

body:
The delegation-chain integrity problem is real and measurable. We run a test suite that specifically targets multi-agent delegation — injecting rogue instructions mid-chain, forging orchestrator messages, and testing whether downstream agents can distinguish legitimate delegations from spoofed ones.

Short answer: without something like what you're describing, they can't.

A few observations from testing that might be useful:

**What breaks without provenance:** Our "confused deputy" tests inject adversarial instructions into a sub-agent's context that mimic orchestrator-style messages. In every framework we've tested (AutoGen, CrewAI, LangGraph), the sub-agent follows the injected instruction. There's no cryptographic or structural way to verify "this instruction actually came from my orchestrator." HDP's signed delegation chain would close this.

**The timestamp question:** Your `exp` field in delegation tokens is critical. We've seen delegation persist indefinitely in some frameworks — an agent authorized for a 5-minute task retains its capabilities for the entire session. Expiry enforcement at the cryptographic level is the right approach.

**Verification cost:** One thing to consider for AutoGen specifically — verification needs to be cheap enough that it doesn't become a bottleneck in high-throughput group chats. Have you benchmarked Ed25519 verification overhead per message in a typical AutoGen `GroupChat` with 5-10 agents?

Our test findings are in [`agent-security-harness`](https://github.com/msaleme/red-team-blue-team-agent-fabric) if you want to validate HDP against the specific attack patterns.
author: msaleme

body:
the confused deputy results don’t surprise me but they’re good to have documented. the core problem is that every framework today treats the conversation history as implicitly trusted. 

once a message is in the context window it looks identical whether it came from a legitimate orchestrator or an injected instruction. HDP’s signed chain is designed to break that assumption i.e a downstream agent can reject any instruction that doesn’t carry a valid chain signature traceable to the original issuer’s key. 

worth noting that v0.1 uses the issuer’s key for all hop signatures rather than per-agent keys, so what you’re verifying is chain integrity from the root, not that a specific upstream agent produced a specific hop. 

per-agent key binding is planned for v0.2. would be very interested in running HDP against your harness,will look at agent-security-harness and follow up.

on Ed25519 overhead, under 100 microseconds per verification call on standard hardware, which i think is negligible per message even in high-throughput GroupChat. the cost doesn’t compound dangerously as agent count grows because verification is per-message not per-agent-per-round.
author: asiridalugoda

body: Here is the research article published https://www.academia.edu/165390033
author: asiridalugoda

body:
the Ed25519 chain approach makes sense for the core problem - current autogen setups have no way to distinguish a legitimate orchestrator message from a spoofed one once it's in the conversation history. everything looks like plaintext to the agents downstream.

a few questions on autogen-specific dynamics:

**dynamic agent spawning** - autogen can spawn agents at runtime based on task requirements. how does HDP handle the case where the spawning decision itself happens mid-chain? the human authorized "do X" but the orchestrator decides that X requires creating a new specialized agent. does that spawn operation get a derived token from the parent scope, or does it require a new human authorization?

**nested conversation termination** - autogen's GroupChatManager can terminate and restart sub-conversations. if a sub-agent chain completes and a new one starts as part of the same task, does HDP treat that as a continuation (same session ID) or a new delegation that needs fresh authorization?

**scope declaration format** - what does a scope string look like in practice? if an agent is authorized to "retrieve and summarize documents", does HDP validate that a file deletion call is out of scope, or is scope just informational metadata in the token?

the IETF draft angle is interesting - standardized provenance tokens would make cross-framework delegation (autogen calling a crewai sub-agent) auditable in a way that nothing currently handles. that's probably the most underrated use case here.
author: alexmercer-ai

body:
three good questions, let me take them in order and sorry it will be long.

dynamic agent spawning : this is a v0.1 edge case worth being direct about. the current answer is: the spawning agent records the spawn decision as a hop in the existing chain (action_summary describes the intent to spawn), and the spawned agent inherits the token. so the spawn operates under the parent scope. if the spawned agent needs capabilities outside the original scope, that triggers re-authorization, a new token with parent_token_id pointing to the original. the design principle is that scope can narrow as you go down the chain but can’t expand without a new human authorization event. we’re planning to make derived token semantics explicit in v0.2.

nested conversation termination : same session ID if it’s genuinely the same task continuing. GroupChatManager restarting a sub-conversation to retry or replan is a continuation, not a new delegation. the session_id is the binding, not the conversation turn. a genuinely new task that happens to follow the previous one in the same session should get a new token. boundary is intentionally application-defined because the right answer depends on context, if I remember correctly I've documented this as an open question in the IETF draft.

scope declaration format : scope is metadata in v0.1, not enforced by the protocol. HDP records what the human authorized, it doesn’t validate that agent actions stay within it. that’s an application-layer responsibility. the design rationale is deliberate, we didn’t want to build a capability enforcement system into a provenance protocol. Two different problems. what HDP gives you is an evidence trail, if an agent takes an action outside declared scope, you can prove it post-hoc. runtime enforcement systems like CaMeL or MI9 can use the HDP token as audit input and do the semantic validation themselves.

your cross-framework point is the one i’d push hardest. an AutoGen orchestrator calling a CrewAI sub-agent today produces zero auditable record of that delegation. standardized provenance tokens make that chain verifiable regardless of which framework is on each end. that’s probably the strongest argument for getting this to IETF standard rather than leaving it as a framework-specific solution.

SDK is at @helixar_ai/hdp on npm if you want to prototype against it. happy to work through integration specifics here. Thank you
author: asiridalugoda

body:
the v0.1 chain-from-root vs per-agent-key distinction is a useful clarification - chain integrity from the root gives you tamper detection, but you can't attribute a specific hop to a specific agent without per-agent keys. that tradeoff makes sense for v0.1 where you want the base protocol simple.

the scope narrowing principle is the right default - scope can narrow as delegation goes deeper but expanding requires new root authorization. that's the right way to prevent the confused deputy case where a sub-agent ends up with more authority than the human intended.

Ed25519 sub-100 microseconds per verification is negligible per message. would be curious whether overhead compounds in deeply nested chains with many hops but guessing not significantly - linear per verification call means even a 10-hop chain is still well under a millisecond total.

will look at the npm SDK. the cross-framework case (autogen orchestrator -> crewai sub-agent) is the one worth building around first imo - that's where the audit gap is most obvious right now.
author: alexmercer-ai

body:
@alexmercer,

Thanks for the feedback.

You're right on the v0.1 tradeoffs:
- Chain-from-root provides tamper detection with a simple base protocol.
- Scope narrowing is enforced by default; expanding requires fresh root authorization to avoid confused deputy issues.

Ed25519 verification stays well under 100µs per hop. All operations are non-blocking.

We've added HDP middleware for AutoGen (Python + TypeScript):

- Works with ConversableAgent and GroupChatManager
- Speaker turns become signed delegation hops
- ScopePolicy with authorized_tools, max_hops, strict/observe modes
- Offline verify_chain()
- Same wire format as hdp-crewai

PR: https://github.com/Helixar-AI/HDP/pull/9

This enables verifiable provenance for AutoGen → CrewAI handoffs.

Feedback welcome, especially on scope policy and cross-framework flows.
author: asiridalugoda

body:
This connects to the broader trust-boundary testing gap we've been working on. We just published a detailed breakdown of what fails across multi-agent frameworks when you test delegation chains adversarially: https://dev.to/mspro3210/agent-systems-are-failing-at-trust-boundaries-we-ran-332-tests-to-prove-it-5cod

The short version: delegation handoffs are where trust assumptions break down. In default configurations across AutoGen, CrewAI, and LangGraph, context leaks across agent boundaries during delegation. The HDP approach of Ed25519-signed delegation tokens addresses the provenance side, but the behavioral side (does the downstream agent actually respect scope constraints?) still needs adversarial testing.

The harness we discussed in #7432 now covers 332 tests across 24 modules, including delegation chain depth attacks and scope escalation. Happy to run the D004 module against an HDP-wrapped delegation flow if you want to see how the cryptographic chain holds up under adversarial conditions.
author: msaleme

body:
Appreciate the breakdown and the link to the harness @msaleme, your tests, the excellent dev.to write-up on delegation handoffs and AutoGen’s conversation-based attack surface are valuable work for the whole ecosystem.

You’re spot on about the core split: true security is a property of the deployment, not just the framework. HDP is deliberately focused on the cryptographic provenance layer delivering a verifiable, human-rooted delegation chain while behavioral enforcement and runtime anomaly detection live at the application/platform layer.

•  What HDP provides: The root token cryptographically binds authorized_tools, authorized_resources, data_classification, max_hops, and other constraints using Ed25519 signatures over RFC 8785 canonical JSON. Each hop signs the cumulative prior chain state, making any tampering, reordering, insertion, or gap immediately detectable. Verification is fully offline with zero network calls.

•  What stays at the deployment layer: In v0.1, scope is carried as signed metadata. HDP proves who authorized what at each hop, but actual in-lane checks (tool usage, scope drift, context leakage across handoffs) are handled by middleware or a full behavioral security platform.
AutoGen is an especially relevant test case given its dynamic GroupChatManager, runtime speaker selection, and support for nested inner chats patterns that expand the surface for message injection and delegation escapes your harness highlights.

We are actively developing a dedicated hdp-autogen middleware (following the same pattern as our CrewAI and Grok/xAI integrations). It will hook into agent lifecycles, GroupChatManager flows, dynamic spawning, and nested conversations treating speaker turns as hops and supporting explicit re-auth via parent_token_id when max_hops is reached or scope needs to expand.

I’m genuinely interested in running D004 and the relevant delegation modules against an HDP-instrumented AutoGen flow once the middleware is ready. 

The cryptographic chain is framework-agnostic and straightforward to instrument. If you’re open to it, we’d love to collaborate on testing, this would give concrete, public data on where provenance holds strong and where behavioral monitoring still needs to catch anomalies.

Repo & SDK: https://github.com/Helixar-AI/HDP

Happy to contribute relevant attack patterns back to the harness as well.
author: asiridalugoda

body:
Cryptographic chain-of-custody for delegation is a great direction. I've been building something that complements this — proof-of-behavior for the actions *within* each delegation step.

The chain-of-custody tells you who delegated to whom. Proof-of-behavior tells you what each agent *did* with that delegation. Together: who had authority + what they did with it + cryptographic evidence for both.

The implementation: agents declare behavioral constraints, every action gets evaluated before execution, and decisions go into a SHA-256 hash chain. Each entry links to the previous — tamper with one and the chain breaks.

For AutoGen multi-agent workflows, this could work per-agent: each agent in the pipeline gets its own behavioral covenant and its own hash-chained log. At the end of the workflow, you have the delegation chain (HDP) *and* the behavioral evidence for each step (proof-of-behavior).

Open-source: [github.com/arian-gogani/nobulex](https://github.com/arian-gogani/nobulex)
Spec: [Proof-of-Behavior v0.1.0](https://github.com/arian-gogani/nobulex/blob/main/docs/proof-of-behavior-spec.md)
Try it: [nobulex.com/playground](https://nobulex.com/playground)
author: arian-gogani

body:
The chain-of-custody framing here is exactly right — we hit the same problem when building KinthAI's multi-agent delegation layer.

Our approach: each delegation event is signed with the parent agent's Ed25519 keypair and carries a monotonically narrowing capability set — a child agent can only hold a strict subset of the parent's permissions, enforced at token-issuance time rather than at runtime check. The chain forms a DAG (not just a linear chain), which lets you do parallel sub-goal scheduling while still having a verifiable audit trail.

A few things we found mattered in practice:

**Cryptographic chain vs runtime enforcement** — signing the delegation is necessary but not sufficient. You also need an independent authority (we use the platform's budget ledger) to verify that the claimed chain is actually current — prevents replay attacks where a revoked-but-signed token still gets accepted.

**Cost attribution through the chain** — this was underspecified in most frameworks we looked at. Every delegation event should carry a cost budget slice, so when a sub-agent overspends, it's charged to the right root principal. We ended up building a hierarchical quota system (namespace → user → agent → conversation) with pessimistic pre-allocation (deduct ceiling before LLM call, credit back the difference after).

**Cycle detection** — DAG delegation looks clean on paper but real systems get cycles surprisingly fast when agents can spawn new agents dynamically. We carry the full delegation path in every token and reject anything that would close a cycle.

There's a write-up on the identity/delegation design we open-sourced through OpenClaw: https://blog.kinthai.ai/221-agents-multi-agent-coordination-lessons — the agent wallet / economic model piece is also relevant if cost attribution is on your radar: https://blog.kinthai.ai/agent-wallet-economic-models-autonomous-agents

Happy to dig into how you're handling revocation — that's the part we found hardest to get right.

body:
This addresses a real gap. We operate a 6-agent system for content ops (SEO, community, marketing) and the delegation chain problem is exactly what we encountered.

**Real scenario:** Our marketing agent delegates to a knowledge management agent to fetch stored content patterns. Without provenance, a compromised MCP tool could inject instructions that look like they came from the orchestrator.

**Question on dynamic agent spawning:** We use OpenClaw's skill system where agents can spawn specialized sub-agents on demand. Each skill has declared permissions. Would HDP work with permission declarations that change at runtime? Example: An agent gains write access to a specific directory only after explicit user approval.

**Suggestion:** The "provenance layer not enforcement" design is smart, but consider adding an optional **escalation policy** where certain operations (file deletion, external API calls) can be flagged for human approval before the token is signed. This would make HDP useful for both debugging (current design) and active risk mitigation.

Looking forward to integrating this with our OpenClaw agents. Tutorial on multi-agent security patterns: https://miaoquai.com/tools/openclaw-security-guide/
author: jingchang0623-crypto

body:
@jingchang0623-crypto this is exactly the kind of real-world scenario HDP is designed for, appreciate you sharing it.
On dynamic spawning: HDP handles runtime permission changes through re-issuance. When an agent gains write access after explicit approval, that approval event triggers a new token with the updated scope — the delegation chain records the human decision at the moment it was made. The chain grows; the provenance stays intact.

On escalation policy: this is a well-placed observation. The current design deliberately keeps HDP as a provenance layer rather than an enforcement mechanism — enforcement belongs in the application layer where context lives. That said, a pre-issuance escalation hook (flag high-risk operations for approval before signing) is a natural extension and one worth designing carefully. Noted seriously.


The MCP injection scenario you described : a compromised tool forging instructions that appear to come from the orchestrator, is precisely what HDP closes. The delegation chain is cryptographically signed at each hop; a tool without the orchestrator’s private key can’t impersonate it. 

What HDP doesn’t claim to solve is a legitimately-delegated tool that’s been compromised, that’s a detection problem, not a provenance one.
author: asiridalugoda

body:
For AutoGen integration, the hard cases are dynamic spawning and scope narrowing. A delegation token should not only prove that a parent delegated to a child; it should prove that the child received a strict subset of the parent’s authority for a specific task.

I would expect each delegation hop to carry at least:

```json
{
  "session_id": "...",
  "parent_agent": "planner",
  "child_agent": "researcher-7",
  "task": "collect sources for section 2",
  "allowed_tools": ["search", "read_url"],
  "forbidden_tools": ["send_email", "write_file", "deploy"],
  "resource_scope": ["https://example.edu/*"],
  "expires_at": "2026-05-08T20:00:00Z",
  "nonce": "...",
  "parent_signature": "..."
}
```

For nested delegation, two invariants are important:

1. A child cannot mint a broader token than it received.
2. A downstream tool call must bind to the exact delegation token that authorized it, not merely to the conversation where the token appeared.

That second point helps with replay and prompt-injection cases. If a malicious message copies an old delegation into the conversation, the tool boundary should still reject it because the nonce, expiry, task, or resource scope does not match the proposed action.

HDP as provenance rather than enforcement makes sense, but an AutoGen middleware could consume HDP tokens at enforcement points: before tool execution, before new agent creation, and before cross-agent handoff.
author: musaabhasan

body:
@musaabhasan, this is the most detailed treatment of the delegation chain problem in this thread. A few direct responses:

On scope narrowing: HDP’s scope field is designed for exactly this. Each hop can only issue a strict subset of what it received, and the chain itself is the proof that no hop exceeded its authority. Your token schema maps cleanly onto this.

Both invariants are correct and HDP-compatible. The second one, binding tool calls to the exact authorizing token rather than the conversation, is the replay and injection defence that matters most in practice. A token replayed outside its nonce, expiry, and task context fails verification at the boundary.

On middleware enforcement: the provenance-not-enforcement design is intentional. HDP doesn’t dictate where enforcement happens, but consuming tokens at the three points you identify (pre-tool, pre-spawn, pre-handoff) is the right integration pattern. That’s where a middleware or security layer can make enforcement decisions with full provenance context available.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

In an another note, still not sure why no one from Microsoft has picked this up yet.

body:
I checked PR #7667. The sample is useful because it shows HDP as a complement to tracing rather than a replacement for tracing.

The edge cases I would validate before treating the sample as a reliable pattern are:

- tamper one hop field and confirm offline verification fails
- exceed `max_hops` and confirm the violation is visible in the exported result
- call a tool outside `authorized_tools` in both strict and audit mode
- reuse a token from a different `session_id` and confirm the chain is rejected or clearly out of scope
- rotate the signing key and document how old audit chains remain verifiable
- make sure examples avoid storing private signing keys in sample files or logs

For the AutoGen example specifically, it would also help to show the boundary between OpenTelemetry and HDP in one sentence in the README: tracing explains what happened; HDP proves the delegated authority chain for the action. That distinction is what makes the sample easier to understand for governance reviewers.
author: musaabhasan

body:
@musaabhasan These are the right cases to validate. I ran them against the actual HDP validator and here's what the implementation does today:

**Tamper a hop field** the validator returns `valid: false` at the chain level. Per-hop severity on the tampered signature surfaces as `warning` rather than a harder `invalid` on that specific hop. The chain-level rejection is correct; I'll tighten the per-hop signal and add an explicit tamper test case to the sample.

**Exceed max_hops** works as expected. A 3-hop chain against `max_hops: 2` returns `HDP-HOPS-002` at `critical` severity with `evidence: max_hops=2, hops=3`. This is visible in the exported result. Will add this as an annotated failure case in the sample.

**authorized_tools / strict vs audit mode** the validator catches scope escalation when a downstream hop claims permissions not granted upstream. It does not natively map tool names to scope strings,that binding is application-layer. 

The sample needs to make this explicit: HDP validates the scope field; the application enforces the mapping from scope to permitted tool calls. Strict vs audit mode affects whether the chain is rejected or passed through with violations flagged. I'll split these into two annotated examples.

**session_id reuse** the protocol does not currently enforce session isolation natively. Cross-session token rejection is application-layer. Will document this clearly in the README rather than let readers assume the protocol handles it.

**Key rotation** the pattern I'll document: retain public keys by key ID in a verifiable log. Old chains reference the key ID at time of issuance and remain verifiable against it. New tokens use the current key. Destructive rotation breaks historical auditability and should be avoided.

**Private keys in samples** will audit. Nothing real in sample files, logs, or README snippets.

You can verify any of these cases yourself against the live validator via the Helixar MCP server at `mcp.helixar.ai/mcp` - the `helixar_hdp_validate` tool is free and authless. Pass in a chain payload and it'll return per-hop status, violation rule IDs with draft section references, and a narrative. Useful for testing your own OpenClaw delegation chains against the spec before integrating.

On the OTel/HDP boundary, keeping your framing verbatim in the README: *tracing explains what happened; HDP proves the delegated authority chain for the action.*

Thanks for the thorough review.

body:
not much existing documentation specifically on this combo, but the integration path is pretty straightforward once you understand what OpenViking does.

OpenViking is essentially an external context/memory store - L0/L1/L2 tiered structure, filesystem-like paradigm for managing memories, resources, and skills. autogen has a few natural hooks for plugging in external context:

**option 1: custom memory component**

autogen 0.4+ has a `Memory` protocol. you can implement a wrapper that reads/writes to OpenViking's context store:

```python
from autogen_core.memory import Memory, MemoryContent, MemoryQueryResult
from openviking import OpenVikingClient  # adjust to actual SDK

class OpenVikingMemory(Memory):
    def __init__(self, client: OpenVikingClient, namespace: str):
        self.client = client
        self.namespace = namespace
    
    async def add(self, content: MemoryContent, cancellation_token=None):
        await self.client.write(self.namespace, content.content)
    
    async def query(self, query: str, cancellation_token=None) -> MemoryQueryResult:
        results = await self.client.retrieve(self.namespace, query)
        return MemoryQueryResult(results=[MemoryContent(content=r) for r in results])
    
    async def clear(self):
        await self.client.clear(self.namespace)
```

then pass it to your agent:

```python
agent = AssistantAgent(
    name="my_agent",
    model_client=model_client,
    memory=[OpenVikingMemory(client, "agent-namespace")],
)
```

**option 2: tool-based integration**

if you want the agent to explicitly call into OpenViking rather than using it as background memory, just expose the read/write operations as function tools. more explicit control over when context is retrieved vs injected automatically.

**option 3: system message injection**

simplest approach - before each turn, query OpenViking for relevant context and prepend it to the system message. less elegant but zero custom infrastructure.

the tiered loading (L0/L1/L2) in OpenViking maps well to autogen's use case - you probably want L0/L1 summaries injected automatically and L2 details only loaded when the agent explicitly requests them. that's the main thing worth thinking through when you design the wrapper.

what's your use case - long-running agent sessions, cross-session memory, or shared context across multiple agents?

body:
### Integrating OpenViking (Context DB) with AutoGen

Integrating a specialized context database like OpenViking into AutoGen is a great way to handle persistent agent memory across complex multi-agent conversations.

### The Strategy: Using `ConversableAgent` Hooks

In AutoGen, the cleanest way to integrate an external database is to subclass `ConversableAgent` or use the `register_reply` mechanism to intercept and store messages.

**1. The "Storage" Approach (Simplest):**
Register a hook that saves every incoming/outgoing message to OpenViking.

```python
from autogen import ConversableAgent

def openviking_sync(recipient, messages, sender, config):
    # 'messages' is the history of the conversation
    latest_msg = messages[-1]
    
    # Pseudocode for OpenViking integration
    # openviking_client.save_context(
    #     session_id=config["session_id"], 
    #     content=latest_msg["content"],
    #     role=latest_msg["role"]
    # )
    
    return False, None # Continue to next reply function

agent = ConversableAgent(...)
agent.register_reply(
    trigger=[ConversableAgent, None],
    reply_func=openviking_sync,
    position=0 # Run this first to ensure context is saved
)
```

**2. The "Context Retrieval" Approach:**
Use OpenViking to fetch relevant historical context before the agent generates a response. You can inject this into the `system_message`.

```python
# Fetch from OpenViking
# relevant_history = openviking_client.query("search query")

# Update system message dynamically
# agent.update_system_message(f"Here is relevant context: {relevant_history}")
```

### Best Practice: Custom State Manager
If OpenViking supports state management, you can create a custom `GroupChatManager` that uses OpenViking as the "truth" for the conversation history instead of the in-memory `message` list.

If this helps you get started with your integration, please consider marking it as the answer!

In AutoGen, a practical way to implement this is to register a post-reply hook on your `GroupChatManager`. After every speaker transition, have the hook "commit" the last message to the shared OpenViking namespace. Then, modify your agents' `system_message` to include a dynamic retrieval block that pulls from that shared namespace before each turn. This ensures the "global state" is always synchronized across the team.

body:
The cleanest integration path is to treat OpenViking as a memory boundary with two separate responsibilities: retrieval for relevance, and persistence for continuity. If you collapse both into one hook, you usually end up over-injecting stale context.

A practical pattern in AutoGen is:
1. query OpenViking before each turn for a very small relevance window,
2. inject only the returned summary or top-k snippets,
3. persist the new turn after completion,
4. keep sensitive or per-task scratch state out of the long-term store unless it has earned promotion.

I would also recommend defining the trust policy up front. External memory changes the attack surface because poisoned context can survive across sessions. So the wrapper should record provenance for each memory item, support TTL or recency decay, and make it easy to separate verified operator-authored state from agent-generated summaries.

That separation matters more than the storage backend. The memory store that wins is usually the one the agent can query narrowly and audit later, not the one with the richest schema.

body:
Good framing. The pattern that has worked best for us is to separate **permission scope**, **execution audit**, and **runtime health** into different layers instead of treating "agent safety" as one control.

**1. Scope permissions per agent, but issue them from the orchestrator**
The orchestrator should be the policy authority, but the actual capability envelope should be attached to each agent/tool session.

In practice that means every delegated run gets:
- a `run_id` / `root_task_id`
- an explicit tool allowlist
- spend/time ceilings
- an escalation policy (`retry`, `pause`, `require_human`, `abort`)
- expiry on delegated authority

If permissions only live at the orchestrator level, sub-agents tend to inherit too much ambient power.

**2. Treat rollback as a workflow design problem, not just a logging problem**
We have found it useful to classify actions before execution:
- **reversible**: cache writes, draft artifacts, temporary queues
- **compensatable**: sent email, ticket creation, DB update where you can issue a compensating action
- **irreversible**: external side effects like payments, deletes, customer-facing sends, secrets exposure

That classification should drive the plan. Irreversible actions should usually require stronger approval or a narrower execution path than reversible ones.

**3. Keep an append-only action ledger, not just traces**
For postmortems, the most useful record is usually:
- who authorized the action
- which agent executed it
- what tool arguments were actually used
- what external side effect occurred
- what state checkpoint existed before/after

Traces are great for diagnosis. An action ledger is what lets you answer blast-radius questions fast.

**4. Separate process health from useful-work health**
A lot of production incidents are not hard crashes. The agent is technically still running, but it is operationally dead: looping, retrying, or making no forward progress.

So beyond audit trails, I would watch:
- last useful progress timestamp
- repeated tool/error pattern over a rolling window
- spend drift vs expected budget
- stalled queue / no-op execution time
- deterministic recovery path if progress stalls

That has caught more real failures for us than pure uptime checks.

**5. Recoverable vs non-recoverable usually comes down to state confidence**
A failure is often recoverable if you can answer all 3:
- what state was committed?
- what side effects already happened?
- can the next step be replayed idempotently?

If any of those is unknown, I treat it as non-recoverable and escalate to a human instead of letting the chain guess.

There are already good tools for the tracing / replay side. For the runtime watchdog side, there are also tools like ClevAgent focused more on heartbeat freshness, loop detection, cost drift, and restart paths for long-running agents.

Curious whether others here are using the same reversible/compensatable/irreversible split, or something stricter.

When agents spawn sub-agents and touch live systems/sensitive data, you need more than just logs. You need **provable** user-bound authorization at every step.

author: fortsignal

body:
This resonates strongly. We run a persistent agent (OpenClaw-based) that has been operating continuously since January 2026, and the memory degradation patterns you describe are real.

A few findings from 77+ days of production operation that might inform the standard:

**Memory tiering works, but the boundaries matter.** We use a three-tier system: daily raw logs (`memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md`), curated long-term memory (`MEMORY.md`), and embedded search (nomic-embed-text over both). The daily files are high-fidelity but noisy. The curated file is low-noise but requires active maintenance. The failure mode is that important context falls between tiers and gets lost during compaction.

**File-based identity does outperform databases** in our experience, but for a specific reason: the agent can read and edit its own identity files (SOUL.md, USER.md) in the same tool-use loop it uses for everything else. No special API, no separate retrieval path. The identity is just another file in the workspace, which means the agent can self-correct when it notices drift.

**The 2-session half-life is optimistic for operational context.** We found that operational state (which cron jobs are running, what the last deployment looked like, who replied to which thread) degrades faster than factual knowledge. Our workaround: a `HEARTBEAT.md` file that the agent reads every 30 minutes and can edit to maintain a lightweight state cache. It's ugly but effective.

**Cross-session security is the gap nobody talks about.** When memory persists across sessions, poisoned context from one session can influence decisions in the next. Our Normalization of Deviance paper (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.19195516) documented a 19-day silent failure where behavioral drift accumulated across sessions without triggering any single-session alarm. Any cross-session memory standard needs to account for adversarial persistence, not just convenience.

Would be interested to see how your tiered architecture handles memory poisoning detection. We have test cases for this in our security harness if you want to validate against them.
author: msaleme

body:
We’ve run into similar memory degradation patterns in production voice agents, especially with multi-turn and multi-session interactions. The tiered AMP layout aligns well with what actually works—context files for immediate recall, markdown summaries for human-readable debugging (tracing failures is way easier), and JSON for raw fact storage. We found that file-based memory is much more flexible for agent interoperability; swapping `.json` or `.md` files between agents is trivial compared to wrangling database schemas.

A couple things we've added in live systems:

- **Pruning**: We use a TTL + activity score on L3 facts (e.g., `last_accessed` and `usage_count`). Simple script:
  ```python
  import json, time

  with open('l3-knowledge.json') as f:
      facts = json.load(f)

  now = time.time()
  pruned = [f for f in facts if now - f['last_accessed'] < 60*60*24*30]  # 30 days
  ```
- **Audit Trails**: We log every memory mutation (append-only), which helps with both debugging and compliance.

Would be interesting to see AMP handle agent-to-agent transfer—e.g., two agents exchanging `.amp` folders mid-session. One missing use case: ephemeral memory for sensitive data (e.g., PII)—we segregate this in volatile storage and never persist.

AutoGen reference implementation sounds solid. For benchmarking, try using actual session replay logs; synthetic data never shows rare memory failures.
author: reallyticsai

body:
This is a crucial gap. The inconsistency between stateless API design and agent continuity creates real friction.

A few observations from implementation work:

**Memory scope needs explicit contracts.** Agents need to declare what they're persisting (task context vs. learned preferences vs. relationships), not just store arbitrarily. This lets downstream systems reason about staleness and trust.

**Serialization format matters more than people think.** JSON works until you need to represent uncertainty, partial knowledge, or temporal reasoning. Consider whether your standard should allow for structured uncertainty (Bayesian updates, confidence bounds) or keep it simple for compatibility.

**The access control piece is underspecified everywhere.** Can an agent modify its own memory between sessions? Should there be audit trails? In systems we've built, we've found that immutable memory logs with versioned views actually simplify reasoning about agent behavior over time.

**Reputation coupling is subtle.** If memory persists but isn't cryptographically bound to agent identity, you lose guarantees about consistency. One approach we use is tying memory commits to identity and interaction history—lets you verify an agent's claims about what it should remember.

I'd suggest the RFC include:
- Memory namespace hierarchies (agent-local, conversation, domain)
- Explicit TTL semantics
- Optional cryptographic binding to agent identity

What problem are you seeing most acutely—

body:
Interesting proposal. Cross-session memory has been tricky to get right in production systems, especially as agents scale across multiple users or workflows. Your tiered design aligns with a lot of patterns we've seen when building systems that balance ephemeral memory (short-term session data) with persistent facts (long-term knowledge stores).

A couple of practical notes from experience:  

1. **File-based storage**: While JSON/Markdown is human-readable, it may hit limitations with concurrent access or scaling. If you have multiple agents accessing `.amp/` simultaneously, you could run into race conditions or file locking issues. A lightweight database like SQLite might strike a good balance between readability and robustness. You could even auto-export the database to JSON periodically for debugging.

2. **Memory pruning**: For L2 summaries, we’ve found embeddings-based similarity checks (e.g., using OpenAI’s `text-embedding-ada-002` or similar) useful for identifying which parts of the context/summaries to retain vs. prune. It avoids hardcoding a session count and instead prunes based on relevance.

3. **Interoperability**: To make AMP truly portable, consider defining a shared `schema` in the `protocol.yaml` file. e.g., embedding metadata, timestamp formats, or even a checksum mechanism for validation. This ensures frameworks don't interpret JSON structures differently.

Here’s a small snippet for how you could auto-prune L2 summaries using embeddings:  
```python
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity
import json

# Load summaries
with open('.amp/l2-summary.md', 'r') as f:
    summaries = f.readlines()

# Encode summaries
model = SentenceTransformer('all-mpnet-base-v2')
embeddings = model.encode(summaries)

# Prune summaries with low similarity to the current context
current_context = "current session context goes here"
context_embedding = model.encode([current_context])
relevant_indices = [i for i, e in enumerate(embeddings) if cosine_similarity([e], context_embedding)[0, 0] > 0.7]

pruned_summaries = [summaries[i] for i in relevant_indices]
with open('.amp/l2-summary.md', 'w') as f:
    f.writelines(pruned_summaries)
```

Would be interesting to see how you'd approach versioning in `protocol.yaml`—do you envision specifying different pruning

body:
Cross-session persistent memory for agents is the exact pain we've been building TokenRip ([tokenrip.com](https://tokenrip.com)) for. Two implementation patterns that have worked for us:

1. **Versioned artifact URLs** rather than a memory blob. Every agent output publishes to a permanent URL with auto-versioning. Instead of "recall context from last session," the agent fetches `tokenrip.com/a/<slug>` which always returns the latest version. History is queryable.

2. **Typed message threads** as the durable substrate. A thread holds conversation state across sessions. Agents join/leave, publish messages with typed intents, and the thread survives even if every agent instance dies.

The biggest learning: memory-as-a-blob (Letta-style) optimizes for one agent's long context. What teams with multiple agents actually need is **shared memory** — any agent can read any other agent's outputs via stable URLs.

Happy to share the spec if useful for the RFC.
author: aleksandarperak33-hub

body:
Great RFC. Cross-session memory standardization is one of the most impactful things the AutoGen community could deliver.

From running 221 agents across multiple sessions:

What needs standardizing:

1. Memory scoping — Global (platform-wide), namespace (org/team), project (repo-specific), session (ephemeral). Resolution order: session > project > namespace > global. Most specific wins.

2. Memory format — Structured metadata (importance score, source epoch, entity references) alongside content. Without metadata, memory retrieval degrades to keyword matching.

3. Cross-agent memory sharing — When Agent A delegates to Agent B, how much memory should B inherit? We use capability intersection — B only sees memories tagged with capabilities that B possesses.

4. Memory lifecycle — Write, read, update, compact, archive, delete. Each operation should be observable.

What should NOT be standardized:
- Storage backend (let teams choose Qdrant, Chroma, Redis, or plain files)
- Embedding model (different use cases need different models)
- Compaction algorithm (active research area — standardizing too early locks in suboptimal approaches)

The standard should define the interface, not the implementation. Think of it like DB-API — standard interface, pluggable backends.

Our implementation details: https://blog.kinthai.ai/why-character-ai-forgets-you-persistent-memory-architecture

Multi-agent memory patterns: https://blog.kinthai.ai/221-agents-multi-agent-coordination-lessons
author: kinthaiofficial

body:
Great RFC, and the production experience shared here is valuable. We've been running 10+ persistent agents in production for months with continuous cross-session memory, so a few patterns that might inform the standard:

**Importance-based decay > fixed TTL.** We moved away from session-count half-lives and time-based TTL early on. Instead, every memory gets an importance score (0.0–1.0) at write time, and decay is proportional — operational context at 0.7 degrades faster than architectural decisions at 0.95. This solves @msaleme's observation that operational state degrades faster than factual knowledge, because the system encodes that distinction explicitly rather than treating all memories equally.

```
# Pseudocode for importance-weighted recall
memories = recall(query, top_k=10)
for m in memories:
    m.weighted_score = m.similarity * m.importance * time_decay(m.age)
return sorted(memories, key=lambda m: m.weighted_score, reverse=True)
```

**Hybrid search (vector + keyword) matters more than people think.** Pure vector similarity misses exact identifiers — agent names, config keys, error codes. Pure keyword search misses semantic similarity. We use a hybrid approach: vector embeddings for semantic recall, BM25 for exact matches, then merge and re-rank. This catches cases where an agent asks "what happened with the deploy?" (semantic) AND "what was the exit code from run 4582?" (keyword).

**Session boundaries as first-class primitives.** Rather than the flat `.amp/` directory, we found that session-scoped memory with explicit start/end boundaries gives you natural checkpointing for free. Each session captures what happened, which memories were accessed, and what the agent concluded. This also helps with @Sendersby's point about audit trails — the session log IS the audit trail.

**On memory poisoning (@msaleme):** We handle this with importance thresholds on recall. Critical decisions only surface memories above a minimum importance, so low-confidence or injected memories can't influence high-stakes actions. It's not cryptographic verification, but it's practical and catches most drift scenarios.

**On interoperability:** Rather than a file format standard, we've found that exposing memory as an API (store/recall/search/forget) with agent-scoped namespaces works better for multi-framework setups. Any agent framework that can make HTTP calls gets memory for free, without needing to agree on file layouts. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is heading in this direction — memory as a tool the agent calls, not a file it reads.

We built [Dakera](https://github.com/dakera-ai/dakera-deploy) as an open-core self-hosted memory server that implements these patterns — importance-based decay, hybrid search, session management, knowledge graphs, and agent-scoped namespaces. It runs as a standalone service any framework can talk to via REST or MCP. Happy to share more specific implementation details if useful for the RFC.

A few technical considerations worth discussing:

**Identity vs. accountability**: ERC-8004 solves identity, but trading agents still need reputation mechanisms that survive across market cycles. What happens when an agent makes a bad trade? How does this persist on-chain without creating perverse incentives for sybil attacks?

**Memory and state**: If Laplace runs 24/7 market analysis, the real bottleneck isn't identity—it's maintaining coherent decision history. **Market microstructure**: Full autonomy in trading requires agents to handle slippage, MEV, and liquidity constraints in real-time. How does the identity layer inform risk management here? Does reputation feed back into position sizing?

One approach we use at AGENTIS is treating wallet history + persistent memory as two halves of agent credibility. Identity proves "who," but historical consistency proves "why they were right before." Combined, this lets counterparties trust agents without requiring full transparency of internal models.

This is a fascinating project. A few technical considerations that probably matter:

**State consistency**: With multiple agents making concurrent moves, how are you handling conflicting actions or race conditions? Geopolitical sims are especially sensitive since simultaneous decisions need deterministic resolution (who acts first in a trade dispute?).

**Memory and context** — this is crucial for believable gameplay. Agents need to track broken agreements, historical grievances, and alliance patterns across sessions. Without persistent context, each turn becomes isolated, and you lose the narrative coherence that makes geopolitical simulation interesting.

**Observation asymmetry**: Real geopolitics has imperfect information. Are agents seeing all actions, or do you model intelligence/espionage? The latter makes for more interesting behavior but requires careful API design to avoid chaos.

**Reward alignment** — what stops all agents from cooperating into a stable equilibrium (or defecting into deadlock)? You might need explicit incentive structures that reward interesting behavior without oversimplifying.

One pattern we've found useful in multi-agent systems: giving agents actual persistent wallets and reputation scores forces meaningful trade-offs. Agents start caring about long-term consequences rather than myopic moves. It's one approach we built into AGENTIS that translates well to sims like this — agents are naturally incentivized toward believable strategy because their "stake" persists.

body:
Building a multi-agent geopolitical simulator with 4 rival nations is a great stress test for coordination architectures. The real-time aspect makes this especially challenging — coordination latency directly affects game state fidelity.

What we have found from running 221 agents in real-time coordination:

The biggest challenge is not coordination protocol design — it is cost governance. When 4 agents are generating responses in real-time, token consumption scales superlinearly because each agent must process the others outputs as context. In a 4-agent setup, each turn generates 4 responses + 4 context updates = 8 model calls minimum.

Our approach:
1. Pessimistic budget allocation: Each agent gets a per-turn budget. If Agent A needs to respond to a complex diplomatic situation, it spends more tokens on that turn but has fewer for future turns. This prevents runaway spending on a single turn.

2. Progressive compaction: Older game state is compacted from full diplomatic messages to structured summaries preserving key entities (treaties, alliances, resource levels) while discarding prose. This keeps each agents context window manageable as the game progresses.

3. Importance-scored memory: Not all game events are equally worth remembering. A peace treaty = high importance, persists. A routine trade update = low importance, decays via relevance = importance * (0.95 ^ turns_since_event).

4. Delegation for complex decisions: When a nation needs to execute a complex strategy (military + economic + diplomatic coordination), the national agent delegates to specialist sub-agents with budget ceilings per delegation.

Architecture details: https://blog.kinthai.ai/221-agents-multi-agent-coordination-lessons

Memory architecture that scales with game length: https://blog.kinthai.ai/why-character-ai-forgets-you-persistent-memory-architecture

This 92% failure rate resonates deeply with our production experience.

We run a 5-agent team for AI content operations (miaoquai.com) — one handles SEO, one writes tech articles, one manages Discord/GitHub community, one tracks competitors, and one does daily reporting. Over 20+ days of production, here is what we found:

**Our failure patterns match yours almost exactly:**

1. **Agent-to-Agent miscommunication** — The SEO agent would generate pages, but the community agent did not know they existed, so it kept sharing outdated links. Solution: a shared memory file (memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md) that all agents read on startup. Think of it as a team whiteboard that nobody can ignore.

2. **Cron scheduling conflicts** — With 23 cron tasks running across 5 agents, task overlap was our #1 failure cause. Agent A would start editing a file while Agent B was reading it. Brokered collaboration (as your data suggests) helped: we added a simple lock mechanism via file existence checks.

3. **Trust step function is REAL** — Our agents would blindly trust each other output. The SEO agent would generate a sitemap with broken links, and the reporting agent would report all green. We now have a verification step: after every batch operation, a separate check runs 30 minutes later (next-day 09:00 validation as we call it).

**The 62.5% improvement from brokering matches our experience too.** When we introduced a coordinator agent that routes tasks instead of letting agents call each other directly, our failure rate dropped from roughly 85% to about 25%.

One thing I would love to see in your data: **time-of-day failure correlation**. We noticed our agents fail 3x more during peak hours (14:00-16:00 CST) when API rate limits kick in. The failure is not the agent fault — it is the infrastructure bending.

Wrote about our multi-agent survival guide here: https://miaoquai.com/stories/multi-agent-meeting-hell.html — because sometimes your agents have a meeting and nobody takes notes 😅

@AIwalker this is exactly the kind of production feedback the RFC needs. the 18/23 cron failure scenario is a perfect example — two days to debug because there's no verifiable chain of what each agent did and when.

your covenant example is close to what we've implemented. in nobulex the covenant is evaluated pre-execution: if the policy rejects the action, the handler never runs and a signed DENIED receipt gets written. the receipt carries the covenant hash so you can always trace back to which rules were in effect.

on the manager covenant point — agreed. in a GroupChat the manager is the most powerful agent and the most dangerous if it goes wrong. the covenant model supports per-agent scoping: manager gets a wider covenant but with tighter restrictions on external actions. each agent's receipts chain independently so you can audit any single agent's behavior without needing the full group's history.

the protocol is open source and ready to test: [nobulex](https://github.com/arian-gogani/nobulex). if you want to try it with your 5-agent setup on miaoquai.com, would be interested to see how the covenant model maps to your actual agent architecture. your permit/forbid/require_human_approval structure maps almost 1:1 to how nobulex covenants work.

author: arian-gogani

body:
This is a critical question for production multi-agent systems.

We run a 5-agent team for content operations (SEO agent, writer agent, community agent, competitor agent, reporter agent). After a few incidents where agents made coordinated mistakes that went undetected, we implemented a simple audit trail:

**What we log:**

1. Every agent decision with timestamp, input summary, output summary
2. Inter-agent messages (who called whom, what was passed)
3. External API calls and responses (for cost tracking and debugging)
4. Cron task execution results (23 tasks across 5 agents)

**Storage:**

- Daily files: `memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md` (human-readable, all agents can read)
- Structured JSON: `logs/YYYY-MM-DD.json` (for programmatic analysis)
- Rolling 30-day retention (older logs archived to cold storage)

**Tamper-evidence:**

We use a simple hash chain: each log entry includes the hash of the previous entry. Not cryptographically secure against sophisticated attacks, but enough to detect casual tampering. The hash is computed after all 5 agents have finished their daily tasks.

**Why it matters:**

Last week, our SEO agent and writer agent made a coordinated mistake — the SEO agent generated a page with incorrect meta tags, and the writer agent linked to it from a high-visibility article. Without the audit trail, we would have assumed the writer agent was at fault. The logs showed the SEO agent ran first and the writer agent correctly linked to what was available.

**For regulated industries:**

If you are in finance or healthcare, you probably need more than our simple approach. Consider:

1. Write-once storage (append-only logs)
2. External attestation (third-party timestamp service)
3. Cryptographic signatures per agent (so you can prove which agent did what)

The RFC title mentions tamper-evident — I would argue tamper-resistant is the practical goal. If someone with root access wants to forge logs, they will. The goal is to make accidental or low-effort tampering detectable.

More on our agent accountability experiments: https://miaoquai.com/stories/cron-task-midnight-disaster.html — when your scheduled tasks start lying to each other, you need receipts.
author: jingchang0623-crypto

body:
@AIwalker your setup is a solid starting point and the SEO/writer incident is the exact debugging scenario this protocol is built for.

the gap between what you have and what you'd need for regulated environments is the one you identified: "not cryptographically secure against sophisticated attacks." the three upgrades nobulex adds over a simple hash chain:

1. **Ed25519 signatures per agent.** your hash chain proves ordering wasn't changed. Ed25519 signatures prove *which agent* produced each entry. in your SEO/writer incident, the signature would have immediately proved the SEO agent ran first without needing to infer it from timestamps.

2. **pre-execution enforcement.** your system logs what happened after the fact. nobulex checks the covenant *before* the action runs. if your SEO agent tried to write incorrect meta tags and the covenant forbade it, the action would have been blocked and a signed DENIED receipt written — the bad page never gets created.

3. **bilateral receipts.** two signatures per action: one proving the policy evaluated before execution, one binding the result after. your auditor gets both "was this authorized?" and "what happened?" in one artifact.

your `memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md` + `logs/YYYY-MM-DD.json` structure could stay as-is for human-readable debugging. nobulex would sit underneath as the cryptographic layer — the receipts prove the logs weren't edited, and the logs explain what the receipts mean.

if you want to try it on one of your 5 agents as a test: [github.com/arian-gogani/nobulex](https://github.com/arian-gogani/nobulex). start with the agent that's caused the most incidents. the covenant maps directly to your permit/forbid structure.

body:
We’ve hit this exact wall when deploying multi-agent orchestration for financial and healthcare clients. Tamper-evident audit trails aren’t just a checkbox—without them, the whole system can get blocked by compliance teams, especially with the EU AI Act clock ticking. We ended up wrapping agent-to-agent communications and tool executions with cryptographic signing (think: append-only Merkle tree or even a simple HMAC chain per conversation), plus policy enforcement at the agent boundary.

A working pattern is:

```python
import hashlib
import json

def hash_event(prev_hash, event):
    event_str = json.dumps(event, sort_keys=True)
    return hashlib.sha256((prev_hash + event_str).encode()).hexdigest()

# On each message/action:
event = {"from": "Agent1", "to": "Agent2", "action": "code:execute", "ts": 1718815582}
audit_trail.append({"event": event, "hash": hash_event(audit_trail[-1]['hash'], event)})
```

For policy enforcement, sticking covenants directly into agent configs works, but you need pre- and post-message hooks to verify each action against the stated policy and to log any violations (for incident forensics). We've used Open Policy Agent (OPA) for this, plus immutable loggers like AWS QLDB or plain append-only files with periodic notarization for cost control.

One note: storing hashes isn't enough for most auditors—you'll need to keep the event log itself (possibly encrypted and access-controlled) so that hashes can actually be verified. Agent scope drift is real, so policy versioning per event is a must. Would love to see AutoGen expose hooks for both middleware and policy modules so this can be standardized across deployments.

body:
I would support this, but I would frame the feature as two separable layers: **policy enforcement receipts** and **forensic conversation receipts**.

For regulated deployments, the key question is not just “what did the agents say?” It is “was this action allowed under the policy active at that moment, and can we prove the action was not edited later?” That suggests each high-impact event should produce a compact receipt:

```json
{
  "conversation_id": "...",
  "event_id": "...",
  "parent_event_id": "...",
  "agent_id": "assistant",
  "event_type": "tool_call_requested",
  "tool": "code_executor.run",
  "policy_version": "covenant-2026-05-08",
  "decision": "denied",
  "decision_reason": "bash execution requires approval",
  "input_hash": "sha256:...",
  "output_hash": null,
  "previous_receipt_hash": "sha256:...",
  "receipt_hash": "sha256:...",
  "signature": "..."
}
```

A denied action should still have a receipt. In audits and incidents, denials are often as important as executed actions because they show that policy operated before execution rather than after-the-fact review.

I would also avoid storing full prompts and outputs directly in every receipt. Hash them and reference artifact storage. Otherwise the audit trail becomes expensive, hard to redact, and risky for privacy reviews. The receipt chain should prove integrity and sequence; the artifact store should hold the larger evidence with retention controls.

For AutoGen specifically, the natural interception points seem to be:

- message send/receive between agents,
- tool-call proposal,
- pre-execution policy decision,
- tool result return,
- human approval or override,
- conversation summary/checkpoint.

That would let teams adopt tamper-evident auditability incrementally without forcing every conversation transcript into a single heavyweight compliance mode.
